Tensor network manifolds and Riemannian fundamental theorem for tensor networks
Pablo Páez Velasco

Abstract
Tensor networks provide a powerful framework for efficiently representing high-dimensional data and many-body quantum states. Endowing tensor networks with a Riemannian manifold structure provides a natural setting for numerical optimization and analysis. A central feature of tensor networks is their gauge freedom, whose characterisation—captured by so-called fundamental theorems—underlies both their intrinsic structure and the design of numerical algorithms. In this work, we study the interaction between the Riemannian manifold structure and the gauge freedom for several families of tensor networks. Using group actions and Riemannian submersions, we establish a Riemannian fundamental theorem for the tensor network families studied.



1
Introduction

Tensor networks have become a central tool for describing and simulating strongly correlated quantum many-body systems, providing efficient parametrizations of states whose full Hilbert-space description would otherwise be computationally intractable. Among the most prominent examples are matrix product states (MPS) and projected entangled pair states (PEPS), which play a central role in the field of quantum many-body systems and quantum information
[
8
]
.

Beyond their representational power, tensor networks are also closely tied to some of the most successful numerical methods in quantum physics. White’s seminal density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithm
[
27
]
was later understood as an optimization algorithm over the manifold of MPS
[
10
]
. This viewpoint was the germ of several extensions, both in 1D and higher, creating a body of research which is the state of the art in several optimization problems
[
28
,
24
,
2
]
. Since quantum circuits are just another family of tensor networks, even variational quantum algorithms
[
6
]
can be interpreted as tensor network optimization procedures over the manifold defined by their parameter space. This perspective naturally led to the study of tensor networks from the viewpoint of Riemannian geometry. Endowing tensor network families with a Riemannian manifold structure provides a natural framework for formulating optimization algorithms, defining gradients and geodesics, and analysing convergence properties
[
13
,
14
]
. In particular, optimization and sampling algorithms on Riemannian manifolds can be used in this context
[
5
]
, allowing to import powerful techniques recently developed in a rapidly growing area of research, mainly motivated by its potential applications to machine learning
[
17
,
7
,
9
,
25
]
.

A fundamental feature of tensor networks is their gauge freedom: distinct choices of local tensors can lead to the same global tensor. The characterization of this gauge for a given family of tensor networks is known as the
fundamental theorem
for such family. As the name suggests, these results play a very important role both in the mathematical understanding of tensor network states, in their use to understand and classify quantum phases of matter
[
8
]
, and in the design of efficient numerical algorithms. Fundamental theorems are well understood in the case of MPS
[
22
]
and have also been developed for some classes of PEPS (e.g.
[
18
,
23
]
).

The main goal of this work is to identify the gauge freedom of several tensor network families, with the aim of describing it as a nice group action on the manifold defined by their parameter space. We show that this group action induces a projection map from the original manifold to the associated orbit space, with the property of being a
Riemannian submersion
. The points in the orbit space will then be in one-to-one correspondence with the state represented by a tensor network. In this sense, our work can be understood as a generalization of the geometric framework introduced in
[
14
]
, from the Riemannian manifold perspective.

It is important to remark that having a Riemannian submersion, as captured by the definition of
Quotient Tensor Network Manifold
(
Definition

1.15
below), is the key property to apply the Riemannian sampling and optimization algorithms developed in
[
5
]
. It is therefore crucial not only to characterize the gauge freedom of a given tensor network, but to do it via a nice group action which ensures a Riemannian submersion. This justifies the name “Riemannian fundamental theorem”.

We study the following tensor network families:

•

depth-two quantum circuits in one or two dimensions, both with a fixed input or not,

•

matrix product states,

•

two-dimensional sequentially generated PEPS
[
3
]
,

•

isometric PEPS
[
26
]
.

For each of these families, we obtain a
Riemannian fundamental theorem
, relating the geometry of the manifold structure to the gauge freedom of the tensor network representation.

We consider particularly relevant the cases of sequentially generated and isometric PEPS, two paradigmatic subfamilies of PEPS. Our results open the possibility to apply Riemannian optimization techniques with rigorous convergence guarantees
[
5
]
to those families.

Before stating the main results of this work, let us define
tensor networks
,
tensor network manifolds
and
quotient tensor network manifolds
. To do so, we start by defining a
network
, which can be understood as a slight generalisation of a directed multigraph (See
Fig.

1
).

Definition 1.1

(Network)
.

A
network
is a directed multigraph
\mathcal{G}=(\mathbb{V},\mathbb{E})
, where
\mathbb{V}=\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathbb{V}|}
is the set of (labelled) vertices and
\mathbb{E}
is the multiset of edges of the graph. Unlike in usual directed multigraphs, the edges of a network may only have an inbound or outbound vertex, resulting in
half edges
.

V_{1}
V_{4}
V_{5}
V_{6}
V_{2}
V_{3}

Figure 1
:
Visual representation of a network.

Notation 1.2
.

Let
\mathcal{G}
be a network. For every
v\in\mathbb{V}
we denote by
v\leftarrow e
and
v\rightarrow e
the set of inbound and outbound edges of
v
, respectively. We also denote by
\mathbb{E}_{c}
the set of connected edges of the graph, i.e. the set of edges such that they have both an inbound and an outbound vertex.

In particular, the sets of inbound and outbound edges of a given vertex of the network can contain both half edges and connected edges.

Networks provide a graphical notation that enables us to visually represent mathematical objects and operations between them in a simple and intuitive way. In this context, we will use vertices to represent
tensors
and edges to denote
tensor contractions
.

Definition 1.3

(Tensor product and tensors)
.

Let
V_{1},\dotsc,V_{k}
be finite-dimensional complex vector spaces. We define their
tensor product
as the set of multilinear maps defined on the product of their duals,

V_{1}\otimes\dotsm\otimes V_{k}:=\{T:V_{1}^{*}\times\dotsm\times V_{k}^{*}\to\mathbb{C}:T\textup{ is multilinear}\}.

Every element
T\in V_{1}\otimes\dotsm\otimes V_{k}
is known as a
tensor
.

Given two tensors, we can define their
tensor product
as follows:

Definition 1.4

(Tensor product of two tensors)
.

Let
T\in V_{1}\otimes\dotsm\otimes V_{n}
and
\tilde{T}\in\tilde{V}_{1}\otimes\dotsm\otimes\tilde{V}_{m}
be two tensors, their
tensor product
is defined as the element

T\otimes\tilde{T}\in V_{1}\otimes\dotsm\otimes V_{n}\otimes\tilde{V}_{1}\otimes\dotsm\otimes\tilde{V}_{m}

acting as

(T\otimes\tilde{T})(v_{1},\dotsc,v_{n},\tilde{v}_{1},\dotsc,\tilde{v}_{m}):=T(v_{1},\dotsc,v_{n})\tilde{T}(\tilde{v}_{1},\dotsc,\tilde{v}_{m}),

for every
(v_{1},\dotsc,v_{n})\in V_{1}^{*}\times\dotsm\times V_{n}^{*}
and every
(\tilde{v}_{1},\dotsc,\tilde{v}_{m})\in\tilde{V}_{1}^{*}\times\dotsm\times\tilde{V}_{m}^{*}
.

Furthermore, there is a natural map defined on the tensor product of a vector space and its adjoint, known as the
contraction map
:

Definition 1.5

(Contraction map)
.

Given a finite-dimensional vector space
V
and its adjoint space
V^{*}
, consider a basis for
V
,
\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}
, and its dual basis for
V^{*}
,
\{\phi^{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}
. The
contraction map
associated with
V
and
V^{*}
is defined as the bilinear map
\theta:V\otimes V^{*}\to\mathbb{C}
, such that

\theta(e_{i}\otimes\phi^{j})=\delta_{i}^{j},

for every
i,j\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
, where
\delta_{i}^{j}
is the Kronecker delta. This way,
\theta
is defined on
V\otimes V^{*}
as the linear extension of the above map.

With the above definitions in mind, let us present the correspondence between tensors and networks in detail. In order to associate a tensor to each vertex of the network, we start by associating a finite-dimensional complex vector space to each edge of the network,
\{V_{e}\}_{e\in\mathbb{E}}
. This way, to every
v\in\mathbb{V}
we can associate a tensor
T_{v}
in the tensor product of the vector spaces corresponding to its inbound and outbound edges,

T_{v}\in\bigotimes_{v\rightarrow e}V_{e}\otimes\bigotimes_{v\leftarrow e}V_{e}^{*}.

(1.1)

Lastly, as we mentioned earlier, the connected edges of the network are used to denote tensor contractions. In particular, an edge
e
joining the vertices
v
and
w
indicates that the tensors
T_{v}
and
T_{w}
are contracted over their shared vector space
V_{e}
.

To illustrate the correspondence between vertices and tensors, as well as between edges and contractions, we provide the next two examples.

Example 1.6
.

Let
v\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
be a vector—which can be understood as a linear map
(\mathbb{C}^{n})^{*}\to\mathbb{C}
—and let
A\in\mathbb{C}^{m}\otimes(\mathbb{C}^{n})^{*}
be a matrix. Consider their product
Av
, which can be written as the contraction (in Einstein notation)

Av=A^{i}_{j}v_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{m}.

We can represent the vector
Av
using a network with two vertices and two edges as follows:

U_{1},U_{2},U_{3}\in\textup{U}(n^{2})
, where

, and let

Note that in the last example, we implicitly assumed that two neighbouring vertices with no edges linking them represent the tensor product of their associated tensors. This will be made more precise in the following definition. Let us define
tensor networks
and
families of tensor networks
.

Definition 1.7

(Tensor network)
.

Let
\mathcal{G}=(\mathbb{V},\mathbb{E})
be a fixed network and let
\{V_{e}\}_{e\in\mathbb{E}}
be a fixed set of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces. A
tensor network
is a triple
(\mathcal{G},\{V_{e}\}_{e\in\mathbb{E}},\{T_{v}\}_{v\in\mathbb{V}})
, where
\{T_{v}\}_{v\in\mathbb{V}}
is the set of tensors that are in correspondence to the vertices of
\mathcal{G}
(cf.
Eq.

1.1
).

We often denote a tensor network simply by the pair
(\mathcal{G},\{T_{v}\}_{v\in\mathbb{V}})
whenever the vector space associated with each edge can be inferred from the context.

Taking into account the contractions between the tensors represented by the edges of the network, each tensor network
(\mathcal{G},\{V_{e}\}_{e\in\mathbb{E}},\{T_{v}\}_{v\in\mathbb{V}})
corresponds to the tensor

\bigotimes_{e\in\mathbb{E}_{c}}\theta_{e}\Big[\bigotimes_{v\in\mathbb{V}}T_{v}\Big],

where
\theta_{e}
denotes the contraction associated with
V_{e}
and
V_{e}^{*}
—note that, since
e\in\mathbb{E}_{c}
,
e
has an inbound and an outbound vertex in
\mathcal{G}
.

Although networks can be understood as a visual (local) representation of a single (global) tensor via a tensor network, we can also use them to represent
families
of tensors.

Definition 1.8

(Tensor network family)
.

Let
\mathcal{G}=(\mathbb{V},\mathbb{E})
be a network. Consider a fixed set of vector spaces assigned to the edges
\{V_{e}\}_{e\in\mathbb{E}}
and a set
\mathcal{A}
,

\mathcal{A}\subset\prod_{v\in\mathbb{V}}\Big(\bigotimes_{v\rightarrow e}V_{e}\otimes\bigotimes_{v\leftarrow e}V_{e}^{*}\Big),

representing the allowed choices of tensors associated with each vertex of the network. We define the
family of tensor networks with network
\mathcal{G}
and set of allowed tensors
\mathcal{A}
as the set of all possible tensor networks for which the tensors lay in
\mathcal{A}
, i.e.

\{(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{T})\}_{\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{A}}.

Let us illustrate the above definition with two examples.

Example 1.9
.

Assuming that the dimension of the vector spaces associated with the contracting edges—also known as the bond dimension of the MPS—is
D
, and that the dimension of the vector spaces associated with the half-edges—also known as the physical dimension—is
d
, the set of allowed tensors is

\mathcal{A}=\{(T_{1},\dotsc,T_{5}):T_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{D}\otimes(\mathbb{C}^{D})^{*}\text{, and }T_{1}=T_{2}=\dotsc=T_{5}\}.

From the definition of
\mathcal{A}
, it is clear that the same tensor is assigned to every vertex of the network, resulting in a uniform MPS.

In this case, as any quantum gate is given by a unitary matrix, the set of allowed tensors is

\mathcal{A}=\{(T_{1},\dotsc,T_{2k-1}):T_{i}\in\textup{U}(d^{2})\subset\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{*}\otimes(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{*}\},

where
k
is the number of gates in the bottom layer of the circuit, and each qudit is assumed to be a unit vector in
\mathbb{C}^{d}
.

In the two tensor network families shown above, the set
\mathcal{A}
is such that it can be endowed with a smooth manifold structure—and thus with a Riemannian metric. Whenever this is possible, we say that the tensor network family defines a
tensor network manifold
.

Definition 1.10

(Tensor network manifolds)
.

A tensor network family defines a
tensor network manifold
if the set
\mathcal{A}
can be endowed with a smooth manifold structure.

Remark 1.11
.

Note that, despite working with tensors acting on the product of complex vector spaces, the manifold structure considered in a tensor network manifold is that of real manifolds. This perspective is different to the one shown in
[
14
]
, where the authors study tensor networks as complex manifolds. Moreover, since we only consider real manifolds in this work, the assumption that the tensors act on the product of complex vector spaces can be easily modified to consider real vector spaces.

As we mentioned earlier, the tensor network families shown in
Example

1.9
define tensor network manifolds. Indeed, the set of allowed tensors in the uniform MPS family described can be seen as the—real—manifold
\mathbb{C}^{d\times D^{2}}
, where
d
is the physical dimension of the MPS and
D
is its bond dimension. Moreover, the set of allowed tensors in the family of one-dimensional, depth-two quantum circuits corresponds to the manifold
\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 2k-1}
, where each qudit is assumed to be a unit vector of
\mathbb{C}^{d}
and
k
is the number of gates in the bottom layer of the circuit.

Given a tensor network family defining a tensor network manifold
M
, there is a natural correspondence between the points in the manifold and the tensor networks in the family. Indeed, every
x\in M
can be understood as a particular choice of tensors for every vertex of the network,

x\equiv(T_{1},\dotsc,T_{|\mathbb{V}|}).

(1.2)

Notation 1.12
.

Consider a tensor network family
\{(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{T})\}_{\mathcal{T}\in\mathcal{A}}
defining a tensor network manifold
M
. For every
x\in M\simeq\mathcal{A}
, we denote by
\mathds{TN}_{x}
the global tensor which corresponds to the choice of local tensors represented by
x
.

In particular, if
x\in M
is given as in
Eq.

1.2
,
\mathds{TN}_{x}
is defined as

\mathds{TN}_{x}=\bigotimes_{e\in\mathbb{E}_{c}}\theta_{e}\Big[\bigotimes_{v\in\mathbb{V}}T_{v}\Big].

Remark 1.13
.

As we mentioned in the introduction, the gauge freedom of tensor networks implies that the correspondence between points in a tensor network manifold and the tensor represented by a tensor network may not be one-to-one, as two distinct points in a given tensor network manifold
x,y\in M
can result in the same tensor, i.e.
\mathds{TN}_{x}=\mathds{TN}_{y}
.

To illustrate the above remark, let us consider the following example.

for which its associated tensor network manifold is
\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}
. Let

x:=(U,V,W)\in\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3},

be some fixed point, where
U
and
V
correspond to the bottom left and bottom right unitaries of the circuit, respectively, and
W
corresponds to the unitary in the top row. Define

y:=((\mathds{1}\otimes X)U,(Y\otimes\mathds{1})V,W(X^{\dagger}\otimes Y^{\dagger}))\in\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3},

where
X,Y\in\textup{U}(d)
are two fixed unitaries and
\mathds{1}
is the identity matrix of size
d
. Clearly, if either
X
or
Y
are different from the identity matrix,
x
and
y
are different points in
\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}
. Nevertheless, it holds that
\mathds{TN}_{x}=\mathds{TN}_{y}
. Indeed,

showing that
\mathds{TN}_{x}=\mathds{TN}_{y}
.

In conclusion,
Remark

1.13
implies that the map
x\mapsto\mathds{TN}_{x}
is in general not injective. In fact, symmetries such as the one shown in the previous remark are inherent to tensor networks, as tensor contractions introduce a gauge freedom. This shows the importance of having fundamental theorems for tensor networks, i.e. having explicit characterisations of the gauge symmetries of general tensor networks.

Consider a tensor network family defining a tensor network manifold, and assume that some gauge freedom of the family can be expressed as an equivalence relation in the manifold, which can be
quotiented out
. In this case, the resulting quotient space induces a
less redundant
mapping from its points to the tensor networks of the family. Indeed, each point in the quotient space will correspond to the
equivalence class
of a given tensor network, modulo the gauge considered. Motivated by this, we define
quotient tensor network manifolds
.

Definition 1.15

(Quotient tensor network manifold)
.

Let
(M,g)
be a tensor network manifold endowed with a Riemannian metric. We say that
(M,g)
defines a
quotient tensor network manifold
if there exists a Riemannian manifold
(B,h)
and a surjective Riemannian submersion
\pi
from
(M,g)
to
(B,h)
.

Notation 1.16
.

Given a tensor network manifold
(M,g)
defining a quotient tensor network manifold
(B,h)
with associated Riemannian submersion
\pi
, for every point
x\in M
, we will often use
[x]_{B}
to denote
\pi(x)
.

It is often the case that the set of points in a given tensor network manifold
M
which give rise to the same tensor can be related by a
group action
on
M
. Group actions on manifolds are very useful, as they frequently allow to consider the quotient spaces they induce as manifolds (see
Section

A.1
).

From the above definition it follows that a tensor network manifold can give rise to several different quotient tensor network manifolds. Indeed, in the following example we will define three quotient tensor network manifolds associated with the same tensor network manifold.

.

Recall that its associated tensor network manifold is

\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}.

Assume that we are interested in obtaining a manifold for which each point allows us to describe a circuit of the family up to a global phase. To do so, we consider the action of
\textup{U}(1)^{\times 3}
on
\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}
that describes the multiplication of any of the gates of the circuit by a complex phase,

\displaystyle\textup{U}(1)^{\times 3}\times\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}

\displaystyle\to\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}

\displaystyle((\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}),(U,V,W))

\displaystyle\mapsto(\lambda_{1}U,\lambda_{2}V,\lambda_{3}W).

In this case, the quotient space
B_{1}:=\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}/\textup{U}(1)^{\times 3}
—which corresponds to
\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times 3}
, where
PU
is the projective unitary group (see
Section

A.2
)—is such that every point in
B_{1}
represents a quantum circuit up to a global phase.

We also showed in
Example

1.14
that multiplying over the edges of any tensor network of this family by unitaries and their inverses had no effect on the circuit it represents. With this in mind, we can consider the action of
\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2}
defined as

\displaystyle\begin{split}\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2}\times\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}&\to\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}\\
((X,Y),(U,V,W))&\mapsto((\mathds{1}\otimes X)U,(Y\otimes\mathds{1})V,W(X^{\dagger}\otimes Y^{\dagger})),\end{split}

(1.3)

where
U
and
V
denote the bottom-left and bottom-right gates of the circuit, respectively, and

and encodes the gauge freedom shown in
Example

1.14
. This way, the quotient space
B_{2}:=\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}/\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2}
is such that every point
x\in B_{2}
corresponds to the equivalence class
x=[(U,V,W)]_{B_{2}}
, with
(U,V,W)\in\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}
where

[(U,V,W)]_{B_{2}}:=\{((\mathds{1}\otimes X)U,(Y\otimes\mathds{1})V,W(X^{\dagger}\otimes Y^{\dagger}))\,:\,X,Y\in\textup{U}(d)\},

and so every
x\in B_{2}
represents a tensor network of the family up to the gauge freedom identified in
Example

1.14
.

Lastly, going back to the quotient tensor network manifold
B_{1}=\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times 3}
, which results after taking the quotient with respect to multiplying each gate by a complex phase, we can also consider the analogous of the action defined in
Eq.

1.3
. This way, we define the action of
\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2}
on
\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times 3}
as

\displaystyle\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2}\times\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times 3}

\displaystyle\to\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times 3}

\displaystyle(([X],[Y]),([U],[V],[W]))

\displaystyle\mapsto([(\mathds{1}\otimes X)U],[(Y\otimes\mathds{1})V],[W(X^{\dagger}\otimes Y^{\dagger}])).

This action induces the quotient space
B_{3}:=\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times 3}/\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2}
. If we consider the composition of the quotient maps
\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}\to B_{1}
and
B_{1}\to B_{3}
, we can see
B_{3}
as a quotient tensor network manifold which uniquely characterises each circuit up to both unitary multiplication over the contracting edges, and up to a phase. In this case, the quotient tensor network manifold
B_{3}
arises naturally as a composition of two projections, rather than as the quotient space associated with a single group action on the original tensor network manifold
\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 3}
. See
Section

3
for more details.

1.1
Main results

As we mentioned in the introduction, the main goal of this work is to obtain quotient tensor network manifolds which uniquely characterise
almost every
tensor represented by a tensor network, for several tensor network families. We will consider tensors (given by tensor networks) which represent either quantum states or quantum circuits. In both cases, it is common to consider equality up to a global phase. In the case of states since they cannot be distinguished by an observable. In the case of unitaries since global phases disappear under the adjoint action. For this reason, we obtain quotient tensor network manifolds that characterise states and circuits both uniquely and up to a phase.

Theorem 1.18

(Riemannian fundamental theorem)
.

The following tensor network families define a tensor network manifold:

•

depth-two quantum circuits in one or two dimensions, both with a fixed input or not,

•

matrix product states,

•

two-dimensional sequentially generated PEPS,

•

isometric PEPS.

Let
M
be the tensor network manifold associated with any of the above tensor network families. There exists a suitable Riemannian metric
g
on
M
so that
(M,g)
defines a quotient tensor network manifold
(B,h)
such that, for every
x,y
on a open and dense subset of
M
, it holds that

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\text{ s.t. }\mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B}=[y]_{B}.

Furthermore, let
(M,g)
the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of depth-two quantum circuits in one dimension, either with a fixed input or not, or matrix product states. It defines a quotient tensor network manifold
(B^{\prime},h^{\prime})
such that, for every
x,y
on a open and dense subset of
M
, it holds that

\mathds{TN}_{x}=\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B^{\prime}}=[y]_{B^{\prime}}.

In the following sections, we will prove this result for each tensor network family considered. The proof strategy will be the same in all cases. First we will identify the gauge freedom. Then, we will ensure that the group action representing the gauge freedom induces an orbit space admitting a smooth manifold structure. For that, we will show that the action is smooth, free and isometric. These properties also guarantee that the projection map associated with the quotient is a Riemannian submersion. See
Section

A.1
for a short introduction to Riemannian submersions, and
Sections

A.2
and
A.3
for a brief introduction on the manifolds considered in this work.

k
gates in the bottom layer. We assume that each gate acts on two neighbouring qudits, which are assumed to be unit vectors in
\mathbb{C}^{d}
. These circuits can be represented using the network

(2.1)

where each tensor
U_{i}
corresponds to a two-qudit gate in the top layer of the circuit and each tensor
\Lambda_{i}
corresponds to the output state of a gate in the bottom layer. Therefore,
\Lambda_{1},\dots,\Lambda_{k}\in\mathbb{S}^{2d^{2}-1}
, and
U_{1},\dotsc,U_{k-1}\in\textup{U}(d^{2})
. Using this tensor network description, the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of depth-two quantum circuits with a fixed input in one dimension, with
k
gates in the bottom layer is

M_{\textup{1Df}}:=(\mathbb{S}^{2d^{2}-1})^{\times k}\times\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times k-1}.

We consider
M_{\textup{1Df}}
endowed with its
natural metric

g_{\textup{1Df}}:=g_{\textup{round}}^{\oplus k}\oplus g_{\textup{bi}}^{\oplus k-1}
(cf.
Section

A.3
).

We will obtain two quotient tensor network manifolds defined by
M_{\textup{1Df}}
and such that they characterise the output state of the circuit. We will prove that one gives a one-to-one correspondence between points in the quotient tensor network manifold and the state represented by a tensor network of the family, and the other gives a one-to-one correspondence up to a complex phase.

Theorem 2.1
.

Let
M_{\textup{1Df}}
be the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of one-dimensional, depth-two circuits with a fixed input and
k
gates in the bottom layer. When endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{1Df}}
, it defines two quotient tensor network manifolds,
(B_{\textup{1Df}},h_{\textup{1Df}})
and
(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}})
such that, for every
x,y
in a open and dense subset of
M_{\mathit{1df}}
, it holds that

\mathds{TN}_{x}=\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B_{\textup{1Df}}}=[y]_{B_{\textup{1Df}}},

and

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\text{ s.t. }\mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}}}=[y]_{B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}}}.

2.1
Characterising the gauge

Let us first identify the gauge freedom of depth-two quantum circuits in one dimension with a fixed input, both exactly and up to a phase.

Theorem 2.2
.

Consider the tensor network family of depth-two quantum circuits in one dimension with
k
gates in the bottom layer and a fixed input, as shown in
Eq.

2.1
. Consider two tensor networks in this family representing the states
\ket{U}
and
\ket{V}
,

\ket{U}\equiv(\Lambda_{1},\dotsc,\Lambda_{k},U_{1},\dotsc,U_{k-1}),\quad\ket{V}\equiv(\Sigma_{1},\dotsc,\Sigma_{k},V_{1},\dotsc,V_{k-1}).

Assume that the tensors
\Lambda_{1},\dotsc,\Lambda_{k}
are full-rank when seen as linear maps from
\mathbb{C}^{d}
to
\mathbb{C}^{d}
,

Assume that there exists some phase
\theta\in[0,2\pi)
for which
\ket{U}=e^{i\theta}\ket{V}
. Then, for every
j\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}
there exist some unitary matrices
X_{j},Y_{j}\in\textup{U}(d)
such that

V_{j}\propto U_{j}(X^{\dagger}_{j}\otimes Y^{\dagger}_{j})

and

\displaystyle\Sigma_{1}

\displaystyle\propto(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})\Lambda_{1},

\displaystyle\Sigma_{j}

\displaystyle\propto(Y_{j-1}\otimes X_{j})\Lambda_{j},\ \forall j\in\{2,\dotsc,k-1\},

\displaystyle\Sigma_{k}

\displaystyle\propto(Y_{k-1}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda_{k},

where
\propto
denotes equality up to a complex phase. Furthermore, if
\theta=0
, the above equations hold with equality.

Remark 2.3
.

The condition of the bottom states of the tensor network associated with
\ket{U}
being full-rank is verified in an open and dense set of the tensor network manifold.

Before proving
Theorem

2.2
, we state an auxiliary proposition relating unitary matrices and the tensor product.

Lemma 2.4

(
[
4
, Theorem 23]
)
.

Let
U
,
V
be two matrices for which
U\otimes V
is unitary. Then, there exists some
\mu>0
such that
\mu U
and
\frac{1}{\mu}V
are unitary.

are full-rank. We used

in the above equality. Multiplying site

by

and every site

by
U_{j}^{\dagger}

and so we can conclude that there exist some phases
\phi_{1},\dotsc,\phi_{k}\in[0,2\pi)
, such that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\Sigma_{1}&=e^{i\phi_{1}}(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})\Lambda_{1},\\
\Sigma_{j}&=e^{i\phi_{j}}(Y_{j-1}\otimes X_{j})\Lambda_{j},\ \forall j\in\{2,\dotsc,k-1\},\\
\Sigma_{k}&=e^{i\phi_{k}}(Y_{k-1}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda_{k}.\end{split}

(2.5)

In the case when the global phase
\theta
is zero, the proof can be adapted by
absorbing
the phases from
Eq.

2.5
into the unitary matrices
X_{j}
and
Y_{j}
. Indeed, note that whenever
\theta=0
, the phases
\varphi_{j}
from
Eq.

2.4
are all zero. This way, we can conclude that
Eq.

2.5
holds for some phases
\phi_{i}
such that
\sum_{j=1}^{k}\phi_{j}\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}
. Thus, we can define

\displaystyle\tilde{X}_{j}:=e^{i\sum_{m=1}^{j}\phi_{m}}X_{j}\in\textup{U}(d),

\displaystyle\tilde{Y}_{j}:=e^{-i\sum_{m=1}^{j}\phi_{m}}Y_{j}\in\textup{U}(d),

for every
j\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}
to conclude that

U_{j}=V_{j}(\tilde{X}_{j}\otimes\tilde{Y}_{j})\big(=V_{j}(X_{j}\otimes Y_{j})\big),

for every
j\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}
and

\displaystyle\Sigma_{1}

\displaystyle=(\mathds{1}\otimes\tilde{X}_{1})\Lambda_{1},

\displaystyle\Sigma_{j}

\displaystyle=(\tilde{Y}_{j-1}\otimes\tilde{X}_{j})\Lambda_{j},\ \forall j\in\{2,\dotsc,k-1\},

\displaystyle\Sigma_{k}

\displaystyle=(\tilde{Y}_{k-1}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda_{k},

finishing the proof.
∎

2.2
Quotient tensor network manifold structure

Having described the gauge freedom of one-dimensional, depth-two quantum circuits with a fixed input, both up to a phase and exactly, let us now turn our attention to the group action description of such a gauge. Recall that the tensor network manifold associated with this tensor network family is

M_{\textup{1Df}}=(\mathbb{S}^{2d^{2}-1})^{\times k}\times\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times k-1}.

Theorem

2.2
clearly motivates the definition of the following group action of
\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
M_{\textup{1Df}}
describing the gauge freedom.

Definition 2.5

(Gauge action for 1D circuits with fixed input)
.

We define the action
\alpha_{1}
of
\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
M_{\textup{1Df}}
as

\alpha_{1}:\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}\times M_{\textup{1Df}}\to M_{\textup{1Df}},\quad(X,(\Lambda,V))\mapsto(X\Lambda,VX^{\dagger}),

where

\displaystyle X

\displaystyle:=(X_{1},\dotsc,X_{2(k-1)})\in\textup{U}(d)^{2(k-1)},

\displaystyle\Lambda

\displaystyle:=(\Lambda_{1},\dotsc,\Lambda_{k})\in(\mathbb{S}^{2d^{2}-1})^{\times k},

\displaystyle V

\displaystyle:=(V_{1},\dotsc,V_{k-1})\in\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times k-1},

and

\displaystyle X\Lambda

\displaystyle:=((\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})\Lambda_{1},(X_{2}\otimes X_{3})\Lambda_{2},\dotsc,(X_{2(k-2)}\otimes X_{2k-3})\Lambda_{k-1},(X_{2(k-1)}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda_{k}),

\displaystyle VX^{\dagger}

\displaystyle:=(V_{1}(X^{\dagger}_{1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2}),\dotsc,V_{k-1}(X^{\dagger}_{2k-3}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2(k-1)})).

Considering the quotient of
M_{\textup{1Df}}
with respect to
\alpha_{1}
we will obtain a quotient tensor network manifold which gives a one-to-one correspondence between points in the quotient manifold and the state represented by a tensor network of the family.

Going back to the statement of
Theorem

2.2
, recall that we also studied the case when two tensor networks

x=(\Lambda_{1},\dotsc,\Lambda_{k},U_{1},\dotsc,U_{k-1}),\quad y=(\Sigma_{1},\dotsc,\Sigma_{k},V_{1},\dotsc,V_{k-1}),

represent the same state up to a global phase,
\mathds{TN}_{x}=e^{i\theta}\mathds{TN}_{y}
with
\theta\in(0,2\pi)
. In this case, the gauge is identified only up to a phase. For this reason, the result obtained can be written naturally using projective spaces. Indeed, as
\mathbb{S}^{2d-1}/\textup{U}(1)\simeq\mathbb{CP}^{d-1}
and
\textup{U}(d)/\textup{U}(1)\simeq\textup{PU}(d)
(cf.
Section

A.3
), if we consider

N_{\textup{1Df}}:=(\mathbb{CP}^{d^{2}-1})^{\times k}\times\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times k-1},

each point in this manifold represents a tensor network in the tensor network family of one-dimensional, depth-two quantum circuit with a fixed input up to a phase. Rewriting the result obtained in
Theorem

2.2
using this picture, we showed that for every
x,y
in an open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{1Df}}
if
\mathds{TN}_{x}=e^{i\theta}\mathds{TN}_{y}
for some phase
\theta\in(0,2\pi)
, then there exist some unitary matrices
X_{j},Y_{j}\in\textup{U}(d)
,
j\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}
such that

[V_{j}]=[U_{j}(X^{\dagger}_{j}\otimes Y^{\dagger}_{j})]\in\textup{PU}(d^{2}),

for every
j\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}
and

\displaystyle\mathbb{CP}^{d^{2}-1}\ni[\Sigma_{1}]

\displaystyle=[(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})\Lambda_{1}],

\displaystyle\mathbb{CP}^{d^{2}-1}\ni[\Sigma_{i}]

\displaystyle=[(Y_{i}\otimes X_{i})\Lambda_{i}],\ \forall i\in\{2,\dotsc,k-1\},

\displaystyle\mathbb{CP}^{d^{2}-1}\ni[\Sigma_{k}]

\displaystyle=[(Y_{k-1}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda_{k}].

As in the case of the tensor network manifold
M_{\textup{1Df}}
, we can also endow
N_{\textup{1Df}}
with what we call as its
natural metric
, which is defined as
\tilde{g}_{\textup{1Df}}:=g_{\textup{FS}}^{\oplus k}\oplus g_{\textup{pu}}^{\oplus k-1}
(cf.
Section

A.3
). In particular, the metric considered on
N_{\textup{1Df}}
is such that the projection
(M,g_{\textup{1Df}})\to(N_{\textup{1Df}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{1Df}})
is a Riemannian submersion (cf.
Section

A.3
), and so
N_{\textup{1Df}}
is a quotient tensor network manifold.

Motivated by the above interpretation of
Theorem

2.2
, we define a group action on
N_{\textup{1Df}}
describing the gauge freedom.

Definition 2.6

(Gauge action for 1D circuits with fixed input, up to phase)
.

We define the action
\alpha_{2}
of
\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
N_{\textup{1Df}}
as

\displaystyle\alpha_{2}:\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}\times N_{\textup{1Df}}\to N_{\textup{1Df}},\quad(X,(\Lambda,V))\mapsto(X\Lambda,VX^{\dagger}),

where

\displaystyle X

\displaystyle:=([X_{1}],\dotsc,[X_{2(k-1)}])\in\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)},

\displaystyle\Lambda

\displaystyle:=([\Lambda_{1}],\dotsc,[\Lambda_{k}])\in(\mathbb{CP}^{d^{2}-1})^{\times k},

\displaystyle V

\displaystyle:=([V_{1}],\dotsc,[V_{k-1}])\in\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times k-1},

and

\displaystyle X\Lambda

\displaystyle:=([(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})\Lambda_{1}],[(X_{2}\otimes X_{3})\Lambda_{2}],\dotsc,[(X_{2(k-2)}\otimes X_{2k-3})\Lambda_{k-1}],[(X_{2(k-1)}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda_{k}]),

\displaystyle VX^{\dagger}

\displaystyle:=([V_{1}(X^{\dagger}_{1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2})],\dotsc,[V_{k-1}(X^{\dagger}_{2k-3}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2(k-1)})]).

The following two propositions guarantee the existence of a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric on the orbit spaces that result after considering the quotients by the actions
\alpha_{1}
and
\alpha_{2}
given in
Definitions

2.5
and
2.6
, which in turn represent the gauge found in
Theorem

2.2
. The Riemannian metrics on the quotient tensor network manifolds are such that the projection maps are Riemannian submersions. For this, we will prove that
\alpha_{1}
and
\alpha_{2}
are smooth, free and isometric actions, in which case the result will simply follow from
Proposition

A.9
. See
Fig.

2
for a visual representation of the setting considered.

M_{\textup{1Df}}
B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}}
/\;\textup{PU}(d)^{2(k-1)}
/\;\textup{U}(1)^{\times 2k-1}
B_{\textup{1Df}}
/\;\textup{U}(d)^{2(k-1)}
N_{\textup{1Df}}

Figure 2
:
Sketch of the three quotient tensor network manifolds associated with one-dimensional, depth-two quantum circuits with a fixed input. Each arrow represents a Riemannian submersion induced by a group action.

Proposition 2.7
.

Let
M_{\textup{1Df}}
be endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{1Df}}
. Consider the action
\alpha_{1}
of
\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
M_{\textup{1Df}}
as given in
Definition

2.5
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h_{\textup{1Df}}
on
B_{\textup{1Df}}:=M_{\textup{1Df}}/\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
for which the projection
(M_{\textup{1Df}},g_{\textup{1Df}})\to(B_{\textup{1Df}},h_{\textup{1Df}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

Proof.

First, it is known that matrix multiplication is a smooth map, and so
\alpha_{1}
is smooth. Now, as
M_{\textup{1Df}}
is endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{1Df}}
, which is the product of the round metric and the bi-invariant metric, it follows from
Propositions

A.17
and
A.15
that
\alpha_{1}
is an isometric action, as it is defined as unitary matrix multiplication in every component.

In order to conclude the proof, it only remains to show that the action is free. For this, let
V\in\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times k-1}
,
\Lambda\in(\mathbb{S}^{2d^{2}-1})^{\times k}
and assume that there exists an element
X\in\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
such that

VX^{\dagger}=V,\ \textup{and}\ X\Lambda=\Lambda,

where we are using the same notation as in
Definition

2.5
. Then, for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}
it holds that

V_{i}(X^{\dagger}_{2i-1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2i})=V_{i},

which in particular implies that for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}
there exists some
\lambda_{i}\in\textup{U}(1)
such that

X_{2i-1}=\lambda_{i}\mathds{1},\ X_{2i}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{i}}\mathds{1}.

(2.6)

Moreover, from the assumption that

X\Lambda=\Lambda,

we know that

\displaystyle(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})\Lambda_{1}

\displaystyle=\Lambda_{1},

\displaystyle(X_{2i}\otimes X_{2i+1})\Lambda_{i}

\displaystyle=\Lambda_{i},\quad\forall i\in\{2,\dotsc k-1\},

\displaystyle(X_{2(k-1)}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda_{k}

\displaystyle=\Lambda_{k}.

These equalities, along with
Eq.

2.6
, automatically imply that
\lambda_{i}=1
for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}
, and so the action is free.
∎

Proposition 2.8
.

Let
N_{\textup{1Df}}
be endowed with its natural metric
\tilde{g}_{\textup{1Df}}
. Consider the action
\alpha_{2}
of
\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
N_{\textup{1Df}}
as given in
Definition

2.6
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}}
on
B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}}:=N_{\textup{1Df}}/\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
for which the projection
(N_{\textup{1Df}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{1Df}})\to(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

Proof.

The action is smooth. Furthermore, it is isometric. This follows automatically from
Proposition

A.18
as
\alpha_{2}
corresponds to the
projected version
of
\alpha_{1}
, which was shown to be an isometric action in the previous proof.

The freeness of the action follows automatically from the previous proof. Indeed, if we assume that for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}
it holds that

[V_{i}(X^{\dagger}_{2i-1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2i})]=[V_{i}],

then for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}
,

[(X^{\dagger}_{2i-1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2i})]=[\mathds{1}],

and so
[X_{i}]=[\mathds{1}]
for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,2(k-1)\}
.

∎

2.3
Proof of Theorem
2.1

The proof of
Theorem

2.1
follows automatically from the results obtained in the two previous sub-sections, i.e. the gauge description obtained in
Theorem

2.2
and the guarantee of a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric making the projections from
M_{\textup{1Df}}
and
N_{\textup{1Df}}
to
B_{\textup{1Df}}
and
B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}}
Riemannian submersions obtained in
Propositions

2.7
and
2.8
.

Proof of
Theorem

2.1
.

First, as we mentioned in
Remark

2.3
, the full-rank assumption made in the statement of
Theorem

2.2
, holds on an open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{1Df}}
. Thus, using
Proposition

2.7
and
Theorem

2.2
we can conclude that
(M_{\textup{1Df}},g_{\textup{1Df}})
defines the quotient tensor network manifold
(B_{\textup{1Df}},h_{\textup{1Df}})
as defined in
Proposition

2.7
, and that for every
x,y
in an open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{1Df}}
it holds that

\mathds{TN}_{x}=\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B_{\textup{1Df}}}=[y]_{B_{\textup{1Df}}}.

To obtain the result for
(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}})
, recall that the projection map
(M_{\textup{1Df}},g_{\textup{1Df}})\to(N_{\textup{1Df}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{1Df}})
is a Riemannian submersion. Now, using
Proposition

2.8
we know that the projection
(N_{\textup{1Df}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{1Df}})\to(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}})
is a Riemannian submersion. This way, we can compose both Riemannian submersions to obtain a Riemannian submersion
(M_{\textup{1Df}},g_{\textup{1Df}})\to(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}})
, and use
Theorem

2.2
to conclude that for every
x,y
in an open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{1Df}}
it holds that

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\ \mathit{s.t.}\ \mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}}}=[y]_{B^{\prime}_{\textup{1Df}}}.

∎

(3.1)

where each gate acts on two neighbouring qudits, which are assumed to be unitary vectors in
\mathbb{C}^{d}
. The tensor network manifold associated with this family is

M_{\textup{1D}}:=\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 2k-1},

and its
natural metric
is
g_{\textup{1D}}:=g_{\textup{bi}}^{\oplus 2k-1}
.

Again, in this setting there exist two quotient tensor network manifolds associated with
M_{\textup{1D}}
which characterise quantum circuits both up to a phase and exactly.

Theorem 3.1
.

Let
M_{\textup{1D}}
be the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of one-dimensional, depth-two circuits with
k
gates in the bottom layer. When endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{1D}}
, it defines two quotient tensor network manifolds,
(B_{\textup{1D}},h_{\textup{1D}})
and
(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}})
such that, for every
x,y
on a open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{1D}}
, it holds that

\mathds{TN}_{x}=\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B_{\textup{1D}}}=[y]_{B_{\textup{1D}}},

and

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\text{ s.t. }\mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}}}=[y]_{B^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}}}.

3.1
Characterising the gauge

Studying the gauge freedom of one-dimensional, depth-two circuits with no fixed input can be easily reduced to studying that of depth-two circuits with a fixed input.

Theorem 3.2
.

Consider the tensor network family of depth-two quantum circuits in one dimension with no fixed input and
k
gates in the bottom layer, as shown in
Eq.

3.1
. Consider two tensor networks of this family, representing the circuits
U
and
V
,

U\equiv(A_{1},\dotsc,A_{k},U_{1},\dotsc,U_{k-1}),\quad V\equiv(B_{1},\dotsc,B_{k},V_{1},\dotsc,V_{k-1}),

where the first
k
coordinates denote the bottom gates of the circuit, and the last
k-1
denote the top gates of the circuit. Assume that there exists a product input state
\ket{\psi}^{\otimes 2k}
for which the tensors
A_{i}\ket{\psi}^{\otimes 2}
are full-rank in the sense of
Theorem

2.2
, for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}
. Further assume that there exists some phase
\theta\in[0,2\pi)
for which
U=e^{i\theta}V
. Then, for every
j\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}
there exist some unitary matrices
X_{j},Y_{j}\in\textup{U}(d)
for which

V_{j}\propto U_{j}(X^{\dagger}_{j}\otimes Y^{\dagger}_{j}),

and

\displaystyle B_{1}

\displaystyle\propto(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})A_{1},

\displaystyle B_{j}

\displaystyle\propto(\tilde{Y}_{j-1}\otimes X_{j})A_{j},\ \forall j\in\{2,\dotsc,k-1\},

\displaystyle B_{k}

\displaystyle\propto(Y_{k-1}\otimes\mathds{1})A_{k},

Furthermore, if
\theta=0
, the above equations hold with equality.

Proof.

The fact that the gates in the top layer of the circuit are related by the gauge freedom described above follows automatically from
Theorem

2.2
(cf.
Eq.

2.4
), by considering the input state
\ket{\psi}^{\otimes 2k}
. Thus, we know that the bottom layer of the circuits are related as follows:

(3.2)

where
A_{1},\dotsc,A_{k},B_{1},\dotsc,B_{k}\in\textup{U}(d^{2})
,
X_{1},\dotsc,X_{k-1},Y_{1},\dotsc,Y_{k-1}\in\textup{U}(d)
.
Eq.

3.2
implies that there exist some phases
\theta_{j}\in[0,2\pi)
,
j\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}
for which

\displaystyle\begin{split}(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})A_{1}&=e^{i\theta_{1}}B_{1},\\
(Y_{j-1}\otimes X_{j})A_{j}&=e^{i\theta_{j}}B_{j},\quad\textup{for }j\in\{2,\dotsc,k-1\},\\
(Y_{k-1}\otimes\mathds{1})A_{k}&=e^{i\theta_{k}}B_{k}.\end{split}

(3.3)

This concludes the proof whenever
\theta\neq 0
. In the case when
\theta=0
, we showed in
Theorem

2.2
that
Eq.

2.4
holds exactly and not up to a phase, and so
Eq.

3.2
holds exactly as well. In this case, the equalities shown in
Eq.

3.3
hold with the extra condition that
\sum_{j=1}^{k}\theta_{j}\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}
. Now, the result follows by
absorbing
the phases in the matrices
X_{i},Y_{i}
. Indeed, it suffices to take

\tilde{X}_{j}=e^{-i\sum_{m=1}^{j}\theta_{m}}X_{j},\quad\tilde{Y}_{j}=e^{i\sum_{m=1}^{j}\theta_{m}}Y_{j},

which allows to conclude that

\displaystyle(\mathds{1}\otimes\tilde{X}_{1})A_{1}

\displaystyle=B_{1},

\displaystyle(\tilde{Y}_{j-1}\otimes\tilde{X}_{j})A_{j}

\displaystyle=B_{j},\quad\textup{for }j\in\{2,\dotsc,k-1\},

\displaystyle(\tilde{Y}_{k-1}\otimes\mathds{1})A_{k}

\displaystyle=B_{k},

finishing the proof.
∎

3.2
Quotient tensor network manifold structure

Again, the gauge freedom identified in the previous subsection motivates the definition of two group actions that describe it. Recall that the tensor network manifold associated with depth-two quantum circuit in one dimension with
k
gates in the bottom layer is

M_{\textup{1D}}=\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times 2k-1},

where each qudit is assumed to be a unit vector in
\mathbb{C}^{d}
. To describe a tensor network of this family up to a phase, it suffices to specify its gates up to a phase, and so we can consider the manifold

N_{\textup{1D}}:=\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times 2k-1},

which we endow with its
natural metric

\tilde{g}_{\textup{1D}}:=g_{\textup{pu}}^{\oplus 2k-1}
.

Definition 3.3

(Gauge action for 1D circuits with no fixed input)
.

We define the action
\beta_{1}
of
\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
M_{\textup{1D}}
as follows,

\beta_{1}:\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}\times M_{\textup{1D}}\to M_{\textup{1D}},\quad(X,(U,V))\mapsto(XU,VX^{\dagger}),

where
X\in\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
,
U\in\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times k}
represents the bottom layer of the circuit and
V\in\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times k-1}
represents the top layer of the circuit. We write

X:=(X_{1},\dotsc,X_{2(k-1)}),\ U:=(U_{1},\dotsc,U_{k}),\ V:=(V_{1},\dotsc,V_{k-1}),

and

\displaystyle XU

\displaystyle:=((\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})U_{1},(X_{2}\otimes X_{3})U_{2},\dotsc,(X_{2(k-2)}\otimes X_{2(k-1)-1})U_{k-1},(X_{2(k-1)}\otimes\mathds{1})U_{k}),

\displaystyle VX^{\dagger}

\displaystyle:=(V_{1}(X^{\dagger}_{1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2}),\dotsc,V_{k-1}(X^{\dagger}_{2(k-1)-1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2(k-1)})).

Definition 3.4

(Gauge action for 1D circuits with no fixed input, up to phase)
.

We define the action
\beta_{2}
of
\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
N_{\textup{1D}}
as follows,

\displaystyle\beta_{2}:\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}\times N_{\textup{1D}}\to N_{\textup{1D}},\quad(X,(U,V))

\displaystyle\mapsto(XU,VX^{\dagger}),

where
X\in\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
,
U\in\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times k}
and
V\in\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times k-1}
. We furthermore write

X=([X_{1}],\dotsc,[X_{2(k-1)}]),\ U=([U_{1}],\dotsc,[U_{k}]),\ V=([V_{1}],\dotsc,[V_{k-1}]),

and

\displaystyle XU

\displaystyle:=([(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})U_{1}],[(X_{2}\otimes X_{3})U_{2}],\dotsc,[(X_{2(k-2)}\otimes X_{2(k-1)-1})U_{k-1}],[(X_{2(k-1)}\otimes\mathds{1})U_{k}]),

\displaystyle VX^{\dagger}

\displaystyle:=([V_{1}(X^{\dagger}_{1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2})],\dotsc,[V_{k-1}(X^{\dagger}_{2(k-1)-1}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{2(k-1)})]).

The following two results guarantee the existence of a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric on the quotient spaces associated with
\beta_{1}
and
\beta_{2}
, which make the projection maps Riemannian submersions. We omit the proofs, as they are analogous to those of
Proposition

2.7
. For a visual representation of the setting considered, see
Fig.

3
.

B_{\textup{1D}}
M_{\textup{1D}}
/\;\textup{U}(d)^{2(k-1)}
B^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}}
/\;\textup{PU}(d)^{2(k-1)}
/\;\textup{U}(1)^{\times 2k-1}
N_{\textup{1D}}

Figure 3
:
Visual description of the setting considered in
Section

3.2
and
Theorem

3.1
.

Proposition 3.5
.

Let
M_{\textup{1D}}
be endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{1D}}
. Consider the action
\beta_{1}
of
\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
M_{\textup{1D}}
given in
Definition

3.3
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h_{\textup{1D}}
on
B_{\textup{1D}}:=M_{\textup{1D}}/\textup{U}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
for which the projection
(M_{\textup{1D}},g_{\textup{1D}})\to(B_{\textup{1D}},h_{\textup{1D}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

Proposition 3.6
.

Let
N_{\textup{1D}}
be endowed with its natural metric
\tilde{g}_{\textup{1D}}
. Consider the action
\beta_{2}
of
\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
on
N_{\textup{1D}}
given in
Definition

3.4
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}}
on
B^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}}:=N_{\textup{1D}}/\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(k-1)}
for which the projection
(N_{\textup{1D}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{1D}})\to(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

3.3
Proof of Theorem
3.1

To prove
Theorem

3.1
we can follow the same reasoning as in
Section

2.3
.

Proof of
Theorem

3.1
.

Again, note that the full-rank assumption made in
Theorem

3.2
holds in an open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{1D}}
. Using the gauge characterisation result shown in that theorem, along with
Propositions

3.5
and
3.6
we obtain two Riemannian submersions, the projections
(M_{\textup{1D}},g_{\textup{1D}})\to(B_{\textup{1D}},h_{\textup{1D}})
and
(N_{\textup{1D}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{1D}})\to(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}})
. Lastly, since the projection
(M_{\textup{1D}},g_{\textup{1D}})\to(N_{\textup{1D}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{1D}})
is a Riemannian submersion by construction (cf.
Section

A.3
), we obtain a Riemannian submersion
(M_{\textup{1D}},g_{\textup{1D}})\to(B^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{1D}})
which allows us to conclude the proof.
∎

(4.1)

We assume that the two layers of unitaries of the circuit—the bottom layer in blue and the top layer in pink—consist of possibly different gates
U_{(i,j)},V_{(l,m)}\in\textup{U}(d^{4})
for
(i,j)\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}^{2}
and
(l,m)\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}^{2}
. The (fixed) input of the circuit can be assumed to be
\ket{0}^{\otimes(2k)^{2}}\in(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{(2k)^{2}}
. Therefore each tensor network
of the family consists of two types of tensors:

and so we can see each tensor network of the family as a tuple

(\Lambda_{(1,1)},\dotsc,\Lambda_{(k,k)},V_{(1,1)},\dotsc,V_{(k-1,k-1)}),

where
\Lambda_{(i,j)}:=U_{(i,j)}\ket{0}^{\otimes 4}
is an element of
\mathbb{S}^{2d^{4}-1}
for every
(i,j)\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}^{2}
and
V_{(l,m)}
is an element of
\textup{U}(d^{4})
for every
(l,m)\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}^{2}
. The tensor network manifold associated with this family is

M_{\textup{2Df}}:=(\mathbb{S}^{2d^{4}-1})^{\times k^{2}}\times\textup{U}(d^{4})^{\times(k-1)^{2}},

and its
natural metric
is
g_{\textup{2Df}}:=g_{\textup{round}}^{\oplus k^{2}}\oplus g_{\textup{bi}}^{\oplus(k-1)^{2}}
.

In this case, we can obtain a quotient tensor network manifold that characterises the output state of the circuit up to a phase.

Theorem 4.1
.

Let
M_{\textup{2Df}}
be the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of two-dimensional, depth-two circuits with a fixed input on a
2k\times 2k
square lattice. When endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{2Df}}
, it defines a quotient tensor network manifold
(B_{\textup{2Df}},h_{\textup{2Df}})
such that, for every
x,y
on a open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{2Df}}
, it holds that

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\text{ s.t. }\mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B_{\textup{2Df}}}=[y]_{B_{\textup{2Df}}}.

As in the case of
Theorems

2.1
and
3.1
, the proof of this result will follow from the results in
Sections

4.1
and
4.2
below. We will omit the details in this case. Also note that in this case we will not obtain a quotient manifold that characterises the output state of the circuit exactly. The reason for this will be made clearer in
Section

4.2
.

4.1
Characterising the gauge

In this case, we characterise the gauge only up to a phase.

Theorem 4.2
.

Consider the tensor network family of depth-two, two-dimensional quantum circuits on a
2k\times 2k
square lattice with a fixed input, as in
Eq.

4.1
. Consider two tensor networks of the family representing the states
\ket{U}
and
\ket{V}
. Assume that the tensor network
(\Lambda_{(1,1)},\dotsc,\Lambda_{(k,k)},V_{(1,1)},\dotsc,V_{(k-1,k-1)}))
that represents
\ket{U}
is such that, given a cut between any two rows or columns of bottom states, every state
\Lambda_{(i,j)}
adjacent to the cut is such that there exists an operator acting on the sites marked in green of
\Lambda_{(i,j)}
,

(4.2)

and such that it generates any element in the Hilbert space corresponding to the site(s) marked in blue in
\Lambda_{(i,j)}
. Assume that there exists some
\theta\in[0,2\pi)
such that
\ket{U}=e^{i\theta}\ket{V}
. Then, the tensors of both tensor networks are related up to a phase by the group action given by the multiplication by unitaries and their inverses over the contracting legs.

Although we can adapt
Theorem

4.2
for the case when
\theta=0
to conclude that the tensors are related strictly and not just up to a phase by the gauge described, we will not be able to study this gauge freedom as a
free
action on
M_{\textup{2Df}}
.

Note that the full-rank assumption of
Theorem

4.2
is always fulfilled when considering a
general
state. Indeed, the assumption can be rewritten in the following ways:

Remark 4.3
.

Consider a cut between any two rows or columns of bottom states of the lattice, as in
Eq.

4.2
. Let
\Lambda_{(i,j)}
be any state adjacent to the cut, and let
\mathcal{H}_{A}
and
\mathcal{H}_{B}
be the Hilbert spaces corresponding to the sites of
\Lambda_{(i,j)}
marked in green and blue in
Eq.

4.2
, respectively. Seeing
\Lambda_{(i,j)}
as a state in
\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}
, the assumption above is equivalent to assuming that for every
\ket{\psi}\in\mathcal{H}_{B}
there exists some
\bra{\phi}\in\mathcal{H}_{A}^{*}
such that
\bra{\phi}\Lambda_{(i,j)}=\ket{\psi}
, which in turn is equivalent to assuming that
\Lambda_{(i,j)}
, when seen as a map from
\mathcal{H}_{A}
to
\mathcal{H}_{B}
, is surjective.

This assumption can also be described in terms of the Schmidt rank of the bottom states; we are assuming that the bottom states have full Schmidt rank when seen as states in
\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}
.

Before proving
Theorem

4.2
, let us first state an auxiliary result.

Lemma 4.4

(
[
23
, Lemma 7]
)
.

Let
Y
be an invertible matrix acting on
n
copies of a Hilbert space, and such that it takes products to products. Then,
Y
is of the form
P_{\pi}(Y_{1}\otimes\dotsm\otimes Y_{n})
, where
P_{\pi}
is a permutation of the Hilbert spaces.

Let us now prove
Theorem

4.2
. For readability, all the figures used below correspond to an
8\times 8
system. Nevertheless, note that the proof is valid for any system size.

Proof of
Theorem

4.2
.

(4.3)

Although the states on the bottom layer of the circuits have not been labelled for readability, they could be pairwise distinct.

Let us fix a cut between two columns of bottom states—represented with a dotted red line in
Eq.

4.4
. Multiplying by
V_{i}^{\dagger}
on both sides of the equality for every
i
not in the cut, and by
\tilde{V}_{i}^{\dagger}
for every
i
along the cut we conclude that

2.4
. Recall that the above equality is only up to a phase, that is, for every
(j,l)\in\{1,\dotsc,k-1\}^{2}
there exist some
\varphi_{(j,l)}\in[0,2\pi)
and
X_{(j,l)},Y_{(j,l)},W_{(j,l)},Z_{(j,l)}\in\textup{U}(d)
such that

V_{(j,l)}=e^{i\varphi_{(j,l)}}\tilde{V}_{(j,l)}(W_{(j,l)}\otimes X_{(j,l)}\otimes Y_{(j,l)}\otimes Z_{(j,l)}).

Inserting this expression into
Eq.

4.3
we can conclude that for every
(j,l)\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}^{2}
, there exists some phase
\phi_{(j,l)}\in[0,2\pi)
such that the bottom state at the
(j,l)
-th site of
\ket{U}
, is related to that of
\ket{V}
, as

\Sigma_{(j,l)}=e^{i\phi_{(j,l)}}(Z_{(j-1,l-1)}\otimes Y_{(j-1,l)}\otimes X_{(j,l-1)}\otimes W_{(j,l)})\Lambda_{(j,l)},

where by definition

\displaystyle Z_{(0,l)}=Z_{(l,0)}=Y_{(0,l)}=X_{(l,0)}:=\mathds{1},

\displaystyle Y_{(l,k)}=X_{(k,l)}=W_{(k,l)}=W_{(l,k)}:=\mathds{1},

for every
l\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}
.
∎

4.2
Quotient tensor network manifold structure

As we saw earlier, the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of two-dimensional, depth-two quantum circuits on a
2k\times 2k
lattice with a fixed input is

M_{\textup{2Df}}=(\mathbb{S}^{2d^{4}-1})^{\times k^{2}}\times\textup{U}(d^{4})^{\times(k-1)^{2}},

where each qudit is assumed to be a unit vector in
\mathbb{C}^{d}
. Since we are only interested in the description of the circuit up to a global phase, we define the manifold

N_{\textup{2Df}}:=(\mathbb{CP}^{d^{4}-1})^{\times k^{2}}\times\textup{PU}(d^{4})^{\times(k-1)^{2}},

which we endow with its
natural metric

g_{\textup{2Df}}:=g_{\textup{FS}}^{\oplus k^{2}}\oplus g_{\textup{pu}}^{\oplus(k-1)^{2}}
. Using this phase-agnostic description of the tensor networks, we may define the group action of
\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)^{2}}
on
N_{\textup{2Df}}
that describes the gauge freedom.

Definition 4.5

(Gauge action for 2D circuits with a fixed input, up to phase)
.

We define the action of
\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)^{2}}
on
N_{\textup{2Df}}
as

\displaystyle\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)^{2}}\times N_{\textup{2Df}}\to N_{\textup{2Df}},\quad(X,(\Lambda,V))\mapsto(X\Lambda,VX^{\dagger}),

(4.6)

where
X\in\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)^{2}}
,
\Lambda\in(\mathbb{CP}^{d^{4}-1})^{\times k^{2}}
and
V\in\textup{PU}(d^{4})^{\times(k-1)^{2}}
. Moreover,

\displaystyle X

\displaystyle:=([W_{(1,1)}],\dotsc,[W_{(k-1,k-1)}],[X_{(1,1)}],\dotsc,[X_{(k-1,k-1)}],

\displaystyle\quad[Y_{(1,1)}],\dotsc,[Y_{(k-1,k-1)}],[Z_{(1,1)}],\dotsc,[Z_{(k-1,k-1)}]),

\displaystyle\Lambda

\displaystyle:=([\Lambda_{(1,1)}],\dotsc,[\Lambda_{(k,k)}]),

\displaystyle V

\displaystyle:=([V_{(1,1)}],\dotsc,[V_{(k-1,k-1)}]),

and

\displaystyle X\Lambda

\displaystyle:=([(\mathds{1}\otimes\mathds{1}\otimes\mathds{1}\otimes W_{(1,1)})\Lambda_{(1,1)}],\dotsc,

\displaystyle\quad[(Z_{(l-1,m-1)}\otimes Y_{(l-1,m)}\otimes X_{(l,m-1)}\otimes W_{(l,m)})\Lambda_{(l,m)}],\dotsc,

\displaystyle\quad[(Z_{(k-1,k-1)}\otimes\mathds{1}\otimes\mathds{1}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda_{(k,k)}]),

\displaystyle VX^{\dagger}

\displaystyle:=([V_{(1,1)}(W^{\dagger}_{(1,1)}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{(1,1)}\otimes Y^{\dagger}_{(1,1)}\otimes Z^{\dagger}_{(1,1)})],\dotsc,

\displaystyle\quad[V_{k-1}(W^{\dagger}_{(k-1,k-1)}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{(k-1,k-1)}\otimes Y^{\dagger}_{(k-1,k-1)}\otimes Z^{\dagger}_{(k-1,k-1)})]),

with

\displaystyle Z_{(0,l)}=Z_{(l,0)}=Y_{(0,l)}=X_{(l,0)}:=\mathds{1},

\displaystyle Y_{(l,k)}=X_{(k,l)}=W_{(k,l)}=W_{(l,k)}:=\mathds{1},

for every
l\in\{0,\dotsc,k\}
.

Using this action, we can construct a quotient tensor network manifold that characterises the output state of a two-dimensional quantum state with a fixed input up to a global phase. For a visual representation of the setting considered, see
Fig.

4
. On the other hand, as we mentioned in the introduction of this section, the analogous of the above action on
M_{\textup{2Df}}
fails to be free, and so the smooth manifold structure of its corresponding quotient space is not guaranteed.

M_{\textup{2Df}}
/\;\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)}
/\;\textup{U}(1)^{\times k^{2}+(k-1)^{2}}
N_{\textup{2Df}}
B_{\textup{2Df}}

Figure 4
:
Visual representation of the setting considered in
Section

4.2
.

Proposition 4.6
.

Let
N_{\textup{2Df}}
be endowed with its natural metric
\tilde{g}_{\textup{2Df}}
. Consider the action of
\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)^{2}}
on
N_{\textup{2Df}}
given in
Definition

4.5
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h_{\textup{2Df}}
on
B_{\textup{2Df}}:=N_{\textup{2Df}}/\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)^{2}}
for which the projection map
(N_{\textup{2Df}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{2Df}})\to(B_{\textup{2Df}},h_{\textup{2Df}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

We omit the proof, as it is analogous to that of
Proposition

2.8
.

5
Depth-two, two-dimensional circuits with no fixed input

The results obtained in the previous section can be easily adapted for the tensor network family of depth-two, two-dimensional circuits on a
2k\times 2k
lattice with no fixed input. Since the adaptations are straightforward, we only present the main result and omit the proof. The tensor network manifold associated with this family is

M_{\textup{2D}}:=\textup{U}(d^{4})^{k^{2}+(k-1)^{2}},

which we endow with its natural metric
g_{\textup{2D}}:=g_{\textup{bi}}^{\oplus k^{2}+(k-1)^{2}}
.

Theorem 5.1
.

Let
M_{\textup{2D}}
be the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of two-dimensional, depth-two circuits on a
2k\times 2k
lattice. When endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{2D}}
, it defines a quotient tensor network manifold
(B_{\textup{2D}},h_{\textup{2D}})
such that, for every
x,y
on a open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{2D}}
, it holds that

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\text{ s.t. }\mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B_{\textup{2D}}}=[y]_{B_{\textup{2D}}}.

In order to define the quotient tensor network manifold
B_{\textup{2D}}
, we first define the manifold

N_{\textup{2D}}:=\textup{PU}(d^{4})^{k^{2}+(k-1)^{2}},

endowed with its
natural metric

g_{\textup{2D}}:=g_{\textup{pu}}^{\oplus k^{2}+(k-1)^{2}}
, which allows us to describe a tensor network of the family up to a phase. Then, we consider the action of
\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)^{2}}
on
N_{\textup{2D}}
that describes the gauge freedom, and define
B_{\textup{2D}}
as
N_{\textup{2D}}/\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)^{2}}
. See
Fig.

5
for a visual representation of the setting considered.

M_{\textup{2D}}
/\;\textup{PU}(d)^{4(k-1)}
/\;\textup{U}(1)^{\times k^{2}+(k-1)^{2}}
N_{\textup{2D}}
B_{\textup{2D}}

:
Visual representation of the setting considered in

where each tensor
U_{i}
is a linear isometry, i.e. a
dD\times D
matrix such that
U_{i}^{\dagger}U_{i}=\mathds{1}_{D}
, and
\Lambda
is some unit vector in
\mathbb{C}^{D^{2}}
, i.e.
\Lambda\in\mathbb{S}^{2D^{2}-1}
. Thus, the tensor network manifold associated with this family is

M_{\textup{mps}}:=\mathbb{S}^{2D^{2}-1}\times\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k},

which we endow with its
natural metric

g_{\textup{mps}}:=g_{\textup{round}}\oplus g_{\textup{st}}^{\oplus k}
(cf.
Section

A.3
).

In this setting, we can obtain a quotient tensor network manifold what allows us to characterise the state represented by an MPS uniquely and a second quotient tensor network manifold that allows us to do the same up to a phase. As we mentioned in the introduction, the results obtained in this section can be understood as a reformulation of the results obtained in
[
14
, Section III]
in the setting of real manifolds rather than complex manifolds, and considering open boundary conditions.

Theorem 6.1
.

Let
M_{\textup{mps}}
be the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of injective MPS of length
k
with bond dimension
D
and physical dimension
d
in canonical form. When endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{mps}}
, it defines two quotient tensor network manifolds,
(B_{\textup{mps}},h_{\textup{mps}})
and
(B^{\prime}_{\textup{mps}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{mps}})
such that, for every
x,y
on a open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{mps}}
, it holds that

\mathds{TN}_{x}=\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B_{\textup{mps}}}=[y]_{B_{\textup{mps}}}.

and

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\text{ s.t. }\mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B^{\prime}_{\textup{mps}}}=[y]_{B^{\prime}_{\textup{mps}}}.

As in previous cases, the proof of this result follows from the next two subsections and we omit the details.

6.1
Characterising the gauge

Let us first characterise the gauge freedom of the tensor networks in this family.

.

\ket{U}

\ket{V}

\ket{U}

Lemma 6.3
.

Let
\ket{AE_1}

\ket{AE_2}

to a composite system

\ket{AE_1}=(\mathds{1}_{A}\otimes U_{E})\ket{AE_2}.

In the general case, if one considers two length-
k
,
k>2
, MPS representations of the same state up to a phase, it is now easy to see that the unique freedom is given by the multiplication by unitary matrices and their inverses over the contracting legs. This result follows from considering partial traces in the same manner as we have done above, in a
bottom-up
fashion. Using the fact that the isometries are full-rank (cf.
Eq.

6.1
) we can reduce the size of the MPS by one in each step.

Furthermore, if
\theta=0
, the above proof holds identically with equality.
∎

6.2
Quotient tensor network manifold structure

As we saw earlier, the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of length-
k
injective MPS in canonical form with bond dimension
D
and physical dimension
d
is

M_{\textup{mps}}=\mathbb{S}^{2D^{2}-1}\times\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k}.

If we are only interested in describing an MPS of this family up to a phase, we can use the manifold

N_{\textup{mps}}:=\mathbb{CP}^{D^{2}-1}\times\textup{PV}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k},

which we endow with its
natural metric

\tilde{g}_{\textup{mps}}:=g_{\textup{FS}}\oplus g_{\textup{pst}}^{\oplus k}
(cf.
Section

A.3
).

Let us now define two actions, one on
M_{\textup{mps}}
and the other on
N_{\textup{mps}}
, which describe the gauge freedom identified in the previous subsection.

Definition 6.4

(Gauge action on matrix product states)
.

We define the action
\delta_{1}
of
\textup{U}(D)^{\times k}
on
M_{\textup{mps}}
as

\textup{U}(D)^{\times k}\times M_{\textup{mps}}\to M_{\textup{mps}},\quad(X,(U,V))\mapsto((\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})U,XV),

where

\displaystyle X:=(X_{1},\dotsc,X_{k})\in\textup{U}(D)^{\times k},\quad U\in\mathbb{S}^{2D^{2}-1},\quad V:=(V_{1},\dotsc,V_{k})\in\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k},

and

XV:=((\mathds{1}\otimes X_{2})V_{1}X^{\dagger}_{1},(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{3})V_{2}X^{\dagger}_{2},\dotsc,(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{k})V_{k-1}X^{\dagger}_{k-1},V_{k}X^{\dagger}_{k})\in\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k}.

Definition 6.5

(Gauge action on matrix product states, up to phase)
.

We define the action
\delta_{2}
of
\textup{PU}(D)^{\times k}
on
N_{\textup{mps}}
as

\displaystyle\textup{PU}(D)^{\times k}\times N_{\textup{mps}}\to N_{\textup{mps}},\quad(X,([U],V))\mapsto([(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{1})U],XV),

where

X=([X_{1}],\dotsc,[X_{k}])\in\textup{PU}(D)^{\times k},\quad U\in\mathbb{CP}^{D^{2}-1},\quad V=([V_{1}],\dotsc,[V_{k}])\in\textup{PV}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k},

and

XV:=([(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{2})V_{1}X^{\dagger}_{1}],[(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{3})V_{2}X^{\dagger}_{2}],\dotsc,[(\mathds{1}\otimes X_{k})V_{k-1}X^{\dagger}_{k-1}],[V_{k}X^{\dagger}_{k}]).

Again, these two actions allow us to obtain the quotient tensor network manifolds that characterise the state represented by an MPS of this family both uniquely and up to a phase. For a visual representation of the setting considered, see
Fig.

6
.

M_{\textup{mps}}
N_{\textup{mps}}
B^{\prime}_{\textup{mps}}
/\;\textup{PU}(D)^{\times k}
/\;\textup{U}(1)^{\times k+1}
B_{\textup{mps}}
/\;\textup{U}(D)^{\times k}

Figure 6
:
Visual representation of the setting considered in
Propositions

6.7
and
6.6
.

Proposition 6.6
.

Let
M_{\textup{mps}}
be endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{mps}}
. Consider the action
\delta_{1}
of
\textup{U}(D)^{\times k}
on
M_{\textup{mps}}
given in
Definition

6.4
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h_{\textup{mps}}
on
B_{\textup{mps}}:=M_{\textup{mps}}/\textup{U}(D)^{\times k}
for which the projection
(M_{\textup{mps}},g_{\textup{mps}})\to(B_{\textup{mps}},h_{\textup{mps}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

Proof.

The action is smooth. To see that it is isometric, recall that the multiplication by unitary matrices is an isometry both on the sphere endowed with the round metric and on the unitary group endowed with its bi-invariant metric (cf.
Propositions

A.15
and
A.17
). Thus, using
Proposition

A.18
we can conclude that multiplying by a projective unitary matrix is an isometric action on
\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})
whenever it is endowed with
g_{\textup{st}}
.

It remains to show that the action is free. For this, let
V\in\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k}
and assume that there exists an element
X\in\textup{U}(D)^{\times k}
such that

XV=V.

In particular

V_{k}X_{k}^{\dagger}=V_{k},

which implies that
X_{k}=\mathds{1}
, as
V_{k}^{\dagger}V_{k}=\mathds{1}
. Looking at the
k-1
-th coordinate of
V
, we now see that
V_{k-1}X^{\dagger}_{k-1}=V_{k-1}
. Following the same reasoning, we can conclude that
X_{i}=\mathds{1}
for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}
, finishing the proof.
∎

Proposition 6.7
.

Let
N_{\textup{mps}}
be endowed with its natural metric
\tilde{g}_{\textup{mps}}
. Consider the action
\delta_{2}
of
\textup{PU}(D)^{\times k}
on
N_{\textup{mps}}
as given in
Definition

6.5
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h^{\prime}
on
B^{\prime}_{\textup{mps}}:=N_{\textup{mps}}/\textup{PU}(D)^{\times k}
for which the projection
(N_{\textup{mps}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{mps}})\to(B^{\prime}_{\textup{mps}},h^{\prime}_{\textup{mps}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

Proof.

The proof of this result can be easily obtained from that of the previous proposition.
∎

7
Two-dimensional sequentially generated states

Let us now consider the tensor network family of two-dimensional sequentially generated states
[
3
]
with bond dimension
D
and physical dimension
d
on an
n\times(k+2)
lattice. Every tensor network of this family is constructed as follows: first, consider
n
injective MPS of length
k
in canonical form with bond dimension
D
and physical dimension
d
, arranged as the rows of the lattice (see
Fig.

7(a)
). On top of the MPS rows, consider unitaries stacked along the columns of the lattice, leaving the rightmost leg of every MPS untouched (see Figure (
7(b)
)).

(a)

(b)

Figure 7
:
Visual representation of a two-dimensional sequentially generated state. The figure on the left-hand side shows the MPSs arranged along the rows of the lattice, and the figure on the right-hand side shows the state with the unitaries stacked along the columns of the lattice.

In this case, we also promote the boundary legs of each MPS to physical legs. Also note that we are not assuming that the state is translationally invariant; each tensor of the tensor network can be different from the rest. The tensor network manifold associated with this family is

M_{\textup{seq}}:=(\mathbb{S}^{2D^{2}-1})^{\times n}\times\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times nk}\times\textup{U}(D^{2})^{\times n-1}\times\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times k(n-1)},

which we endow with its
natural metric

g_{\textup{seq}}:=g_{\textup{round}}^{\oplus n}\oplus g_{\textup{st}}^{\oplus nk}\oplus g_{\textup{bi}}^{\oplus(k+1)(n-1)}
.

In this case, similarly to when we considered two-dimensional circuits, we can only find a quotient tensor network manifold that characterises sequentially generated states up to a phase. The proof will follow from the results of the next two subsections.

Theorem 7.1
.

Let
M_{\textup{seq}}
be the tensor network manifold associated with two-dimensional sequentially generated states with bond dimension
D
and physical dimension
d\leq D^{2}
on an
n\times(k+2)
lattice. When endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{seq}}
, it defines a quotient tensor network manifold,
(B_{\textup{seq}},h_{\textup{seq}})
such that, for every
x,y
on a open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{seq}}
, it holds that

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\text{ s.t. }\mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B_{\textup{seq}}}=[y]_{B_{\textup{seq}}}.

to

(7.1)

Further assume that the bottom state of every MPS is full-rank when seen as a map from
\mathbb{C}^{D}
to
\mathbb{C}^{D}
. Let
\theta\in[0,2\pi)
be such that
\ket{U}=e^{i\theta}\ket{V}
. Then, the tensors of the tensor networks associated with
\ket{U}
and
\ket{V}
are related, up to a phase, by the multiplication by unitaries and their inverses over the contracting edges.

Proof of
Theorem

7.2
.

Following an analogous approach to that used for matrix product states, we analyse the gauge freedom of two-dimensional sequentially generated states by induction in the number of rows. This way, consider two two-dimensional sequentially generated states on a
2\times(k+1)
lattice representing the same state up to a phase,

(7.3)

where

C_{1}:=A_{1}^{\dagger}B_{1}.

In particular, using the full-rank assumption of the isometries
V_{1},\dotsc,V_{2k}
,
Eq.

7.3
implies that for every
\ket{\phi},\ket{\varphi}\in\mathbb{C}^{D}
there exist
\ket{\alpha},\ket{\beta}\in\mathbb{C}^{D}
such that

C_{1}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{\varphi})=\ket{\alpha}\otimes\ket{\beta},

i.e.
C_{1}
maps products to products. By
Lemma

4.4
we can conclude that there exist two unitary matrices
X_{1},X_{2}\in\textup{U}(D)
such that

C_{1}=P^{1}_{\pi}(X_{1}\otimes X_{2}),

where
P^{1}_{\pi}
is either a SWAP gate or the identity. Next, for any
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}
, let us choose the
i
-th isometry of the MPSs. In both rows, we group the legs that are at the right of the rightmost leg of the isometry, and the legs at the left of the bottom leg of the isometry; we obtain

(7.4)

where
C_{i+1}:=A^{\dagger}_{i+1}B_{i+1}
. Using the full-rank assumption of the isometries shown in
Eq.

7.1
,
Eq.

7.4
implies that for every
\ket{\phi},\ket{\varphi}\in\mathbb{C}^{D}
there exist
\ket{\alpha},\ket{\beta}\in\mathbb{C}^{D}
such that

C_{i+1}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{\varphi})=\ket{\alpha}\otimes\ket{\beta},

and so there exist two unitaries
X_{2i+1},X_{2(i+1)}
such that
C_{i+1}=P^{i+1}_{\pi}(X_{2i+1}\otimes X_{2(i+1)})
, where
P^{i+1}_{\pi}
is either the SWAP gate or the identity. This allows us to rewrite
Eq.

7.2
as

Lemma

6.3
there exists a unitary matrix

Looking at this last identity, since
P^{k+1}_{\pi}
is either the SWAP gate or the identity, we know that it must be the case that either

\propto
U_{k}
Y_{k}
U_{2k}
V_{k}
V_{2k}
\propto
U_{k}
Y_{k}
U_{2k}
V_{k}
V_{2k}
or

In either case by the full-rank assumption on the isometries, this means that
Y_{k}
maps product states to product states and so by
Lemma

4.4
it must be the composition of a product unitary with either a SWAP gate or the identity. This means that either

(7.8)

Note that the last three scenarios cannot happen. Indeed, let
v_{1},v_{2}
and

where we have used arrows to explicit that we are seeing each tensor network as a linear map from the Hilbert spaces associated with the inbound edges to that associated with the outbound edge. Whilst the right-hand side of the above identities is always a surjective linear map by assumption, the left-hand side cannot be, yielding a contradiction. Thus, it must be the case that
Y_{k}=Y_{k}^{1}\otimes Y_{k}^{2}
for some unitary matrices
Y_{k}^{1},Y_{k}^{2}\in\textup{U}(D)
, and that
P^{k+1}_{\pi}=\mathds{1}
.

Inserting this into
Eq.

7.7
for
i=k-1
we can continue the same reasoning to conclude that
P^{k}_{\pi}
is also the identity matrix and that
Y_{k-1}
is of the form
Y_{k-1}^{1}\otimes Y^{2}_{k-1}
for some unitary matrices
Y_{k-1}^{1},Y^{2}_{k-1}\in\textup{U}(D)
. In fact, one can follow the same argument to conclude that
P^{i}_{\pi}=\mathds{1}
for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k+1\}
and that
Y_{i}=Y_{i}^{1}\otimes Y_{i}^{2}
for some unitary matrices
Y_{i}^{1},Y^{2}_{i}\in\textup{U}(D)
, for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}
, finishing the proof.

In the more general case, given two sequentially generated states on an
n\times(k+1)
lattice with
n>2
rows, we can group the first
n-1
rows and proceed by induction.
∎

7.2
Quotient tensor network manifold structure

Let us now describe the gauge identified in the previous subsection as a group action. Recall that the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of two-dimensional, sequentially generated states with bond dimension
D
and physical dimension
d
on an
n\times(k+2)
lattice is

M_{\textup{seq}}=(\mathbb{S}^{2D^{2}-1})^{\times n}\times\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times nk}\times\textup{U}(D^{2})^{\times n-1}\times\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times k(n-1)}.

To describe the tensor networks of this family up to a phase, we can consider the manifold

N_{\textup{seq}}:=(\mathbb{CP}^{D^{2}-1})^{\times n}\times\textup{PV}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times nk}\times\textup{PU}(D^{2})^{\times n-1}\times\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times k(n-1)},

endowed with its
natural metric

\tilde{g}_{\textup{seq}}:=g_{\textup{FS}}^{\oplus n}\oplus g_{\textup{pst}}^{\oplus nk}\oplus g_{\textup{pu}}^{\oplus(k+1)(n-1)}
.

Definition 7.3

(Gauge action on sequentially generated PEPS)
.

We define the action of
\textup{PU}(D)^{2(n-1)+kn}\times\textup{PU}(d)^{2k(n-1)}
on
N_{\textup{seq}}
as

\displaystyle\textup{PU}(D)^{2(n-1)+kn}\times\textup{PU}(d)^{2k(n-1)}\times N_{\textup{seq}}\to N_{\textup{seq}},\quad(X,(U,V,W))\mapsto(XU,XV,XW),

where
X\in\textup{PU}(D)^{2(n-1)+kn}\times\textup{PU}(d)^{2k(n-1)}
, and

\displaystyle U

\displaystyle:=([U_{1}],\dotsc,[U_{n}])\in(\mathbb{CP}^{D^{2}-1})^{\times n},

\displaystyle V

\displaystyle:=(V^{1},\dotsc,V^{n})\in(\textup{PV}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k})^{\times n},

\displaystyle W

\displaystyle:=(W^{1},\dotsc,W^{k+1})\in\textup{PU}(D^{2})^{\times n-1}\times(\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times(n-1)})^{\times k},

where the tuple
U
represents the bottom states of the MPSs composing the state, each
W^{i}
denotes a column of unitaries and each
V^{i}
denotes the set of isometries of an MPS of the state. For this reason
W
has
(k+1)
components and
V
has
n
components. Each element
W^{i}
and
V^{i}
is defined as

\displaystyle V^{i}

\displaystyle:=([V^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[V^{i}_{k}])\in\textup{PV}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})^{\times k},

\displaystyle W^{1}

\displaystyle:=([W^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[W^{i}_{n-1}])\in\textup{PU}(D^{2})^{\times(n-1)},

\displaystyle W^{i}

\displaystyle:=([W^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[W^{i}_{n-1}])\in\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times(n-1)},\quad\forall i\in\{2,\dotsc,k+1\}.

Furthermore, for readability, we will write

X=(X^{1},\dotsc,X^{n},\tilde{X}^{1},\dotsc,\tilde{X}^{k+1}),

where

\displaystyle X^{i}

\displaystyle=([X^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[X^{i}_{k}])\in\textup{PU}(D)^{\times k},\quad\forall i\in\{1,\dotsc,n\},

\displaystyle\tilde{X}^{1}

\displaystyle=([\tilde{X}^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-1)}])\in\textup{PU}(D)^{\times 2(n-1)},

\displaystyle\tilde{X}^{i}

\displaystyle=([\tilde{X}^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-1)}])\in\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(n-1)},\quad\forall i\in\{2,\dotsc,k+1\}.

We defined
X
so that each
\tilde{X}^{i}
acts on the
i
-th column of unitaries, represented by
W^{i}
. Furthermore, each
X^{i}
acts on the MPS in the
i
-th row, represented by
[U_{i}]
and
V^{i}
. This way, the action on the unitaries can be defined as

XW:=(\tilde{X}^{1}W^{1},\tilde{X}^{2}W^{2},\dotsc,\tilde{X}^{k+1}W^{k+1}),

where for each column
\tilde{X}^{i}
acts naturally (see
Fig.
