\tilde{X}^{i}W^{i}:=([(\mathds{1}\otimes\tilde{X}^{i}_{3})W^{i}_{1}((\tilde{X}^{i}_{1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\tilde{X}^{i}_{2})^{\dagger})],\dotsc,\\
[(\mathds{1}\otimes\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)+1})W^{i}_{n-2}((\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)-1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)})^{\dagger})],[W^{i}_{n-1}((\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)+1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-1)})^{\dagger})]).

(7.9)

As usual, the above action allows us to define a quotient tensor network manifold such that every point in it is in one-to-one correspondence with a two-dimensional sequentially generated state up to a phase.

N_{\textup{seq}}
M_{\textup{seq}}
B_{\textup{seq}}
/\;\textup{U}(1)^{(k+1)(2n-1)}
/\;\textup{PU}(D)^{2(n-1)+kn}\times\textup{PU}(d)^{2k(n-1)}

Figure 11
:
Visual representation of the setting considered in

.

Proposition 7.4
.

Let
N_{\textup{seq}}
be endowed with its natural metric
\tilde{g}_{\textup{seq}}
. Consider the action of
\textup{PU}(D)^{2(n-1)+kn}\times\textup{PU}(d)^{2k(n-1)}
on
N_{\textup{seq}}
as given in
Definition

7.3
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h_{\textup{seq}}
on
B_{\textup{seq}}:=N_{\textup{seq}}/\textup{PU}(D)^{2(n-1)+kn}\times\textup{PU}(d)^{2k(n-1)}
for which the projection
(N_{\textup{seq}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{seq}})\to(B_{\textup{seq}},h_{\textup{seq}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

Proof.

Again, this action is smooth and isometric. In order to show that it is free, consider some
X\in\textup{PU}(D)^{2(n-1)+kn}\times\textup{PU}(d)^{2k(n-1)}
and assume that there exists a tuple
(U,V,W)\in N_{\textup{seq}}
satisfying

(U,V,W)=(XU,XV,XW).

In particular, for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k+1\}

([W^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[W^{i}_{n-1}])=([(\mathds{1}\otimes\tilde{X}^{i}_{3})W^{i}_{1}((\tilde{X}^{i}_{1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\tilde{X}^{i}_{2})^{\dagger})],\dotsc,\\
[(\mathds{1}\otimes\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)+1})W^{i}_{n-2}((\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)-1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)})^{\dagger})],[W^{i}_{n-1}((\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)+1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-1)})^{\dagger})]).

(7.12)

Thus, looking at the rightmost coordinate, the above equation implies that, for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k+1\}

[W^{i}_{n-1}]=[W^{i}_{n-1}((\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)+1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-1)})^{\dagger})],

which can be rewritten as

[\mathds{1}]=[((\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-2)+1})^{\dagger}\otimes(\tilde{X}^{i}_{2(n-1)})^{\dagger})].

Inserting this into
Eq.

7.12
and looking at the next rightmost coordinate, we can continue the same reasoning to conclude that
[\tilde{X}^{i}_{j}]=[\mathds{1}]
for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,k+1\}
,
j\in\{1,\dotsc,n-1\}
. Using these equalities and the assumption that
XV=V
, we now know that

([V^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[V^{i}_{k}])=([(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{i}_{2})V^{i}_{1}(X^{i}_{1})^{\dagger}],\dotsc,[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{i}_{k})V^{i}_{k-1}(X^{i}_{k-1})^{\dagger}],[V^{i}_{k}(X^{i}_{k})^{\dagger}]),

for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
. Following the same ideas as in the proof of
Proposition

6.7
, we can conclude that
X^{i}_{j}=[\mathds{1}]
for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
,
j\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}
, finishing the proof.
∎

8
Isometric PEPS

Lastly, let us study the tensor network family of isometric PEPS
[
26
]
on an
L\times(L+1)
lattice with physical dimension
d
and bond dimension
D
. Every tensor network of this family is constructed by sequentially applying isometries on a two-dimensional lattice. The order in which the isometries are applied is fixed, and corresponds to the radial preparation considered in
[
26
]
. For example, the tensor network family of isometric PEPS on a
4\times 5
lattice consists of those tensor networks of the form

(8.1)

where the different tensors have been given numeric labels so that they are clearly identified.

Note that, as in the case of sequentially generated states and MPS states, we also consider open boundary conditions and promote the boundary legs of the state to physical legs. The tensor network manifold associated with this family is

\displaystyle M_{\textup{iso}}

\displaystyle:=\mathbb{S}^{2D^{4}-1}\times\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{D^{3}})^{\times 2L-3}\times\textup{V}_{D^{2}}(\mathbb{C}^{dD^{2}})^{\times(L-2)^{2}}

\displaystyle\quad\times\textup{V}_{D^{2}}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}D})^{L-2}\times\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})\times\textup{U}(D^{2})^{\times L-1},

which we endow with its
natural metric

g_{\textup{iso}}:=g_{\textup{round}}\oplus g_{st}^{\oplus L(L-1)}\oplus g_{\textup{bi}}^{\oplus L-1}
.

Theorem 8.1
.

Let
M_{\textup{iso}}
be the tensor network manifold associated with isometric PEPS on a
L\times(L+1)
lattice with bond dimension
D
and physical dimension
d
. When endowed with its natural metric
g_{\textup{iso}}
, it defines a quotient tensor network manifold
(B_{\textup{iso}},h_{\textup{iso}})
such that, for every
x,y
on an open and dense subset of
M_{\textup{iso}}
, it holds that

\exists\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\ \text{s.t.}\ \mathds{TN}_{x}=\lambda\mathds{TN}_{y}\iff[x]_{B_{\textup{iso}}}=[x]_{B_{\textup{iso}}}.

As in all previous cases, the proof follows from the following two subsections.

8.1
Characterising the gauge

Let us first characterise the gauge freedom of the tensors in the family of isometric PEPS.

we can decompose
U
as

U=\sum_{ij=1}^{n}U_{ij}\otimes\ket{i}\bra{j}.

Now,
Eq.

8.10
implies that for every
i,j,k,l\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
, there exists some
\alpha_{ijkl}\in\mathbb{C}
such that

U^{\dagger}_{ki}U_{lj}=\alpha_{ijkl}\mathds{1}.

(8.11)

In particular, for every
i,j\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
,

U_{ij}^{\dagger}U_{ij}=\alpha_{jjii}\mathds{1},

where
\alpha_{jjii}\geq 0
as
U_{ij}^{\dagger}U_{ij}
is Hermitian and positive-semidefinite. Therefore, for every
i,j\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
,
U_{ij}
is of the form

U_{ij}=\sqrt{\alpha_{jjii}}\,V_{ij},

(8.12)

for some unitary matrix
V_{ij}\in\textup{U}(n)
. Putting
Eqs.

8.11
and
8.12
together we conclude that for every
i,j,k,l\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
,

\alpha_{ijkl}\mathds{1}=U_{ki}^{\dagger}U_{lj}=\sqrt{\alpha_{iikk}\alpha_{jjll}}\,V^{\dagger}_{ki}V_{lj},

and so for every
i,j,k,l\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
it holds that

\alpha_{ijkl}V_{ki}=\sqrt{\alpha_{iikk}\alpha_{jjll}}\,V_{lj},

which means that the unitaries
V_{ij}
only differ by a global phase, which allows us to rewrite
Eq.

8.12
as

U_{ij}=\beta_{ij}V,

for every
i,j\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}
, where
V\in\textup{U}(n)
is some fixed unitary and
\beta_{ij}\in\mathbb{C}
,
|\beta_{ij}|=1
. Thus,

U=\sum_{ij=1}^{n}U_{ij}\otimes\ket{i}\bra{j}=V\otimes\sum_{ij=1}^{n}\beta_{ij}\ket{i}\bra{j}.

Lastly, using
Lemma

2.4
we conclude that
\sum_{ij=1}^{n}\beta_{ij}\ket{i}\bra{j}
is also unitary, finishing the proof.
∎

Lastly, we contract both tensor networks against their adjoints leaving the two leftmost legs of
U_{3}
and
V_{3}
open, obtaining that

Y_{2}
Y_{2}^{\dagger}
U_{3}
U_{3}^{\dagger}
V_{3}
V_{3}^{\dagger}
\propto

which again by
Lemma

6.3
implies that there exists some unitary matrix
Z\in\textup{U}(D)
such that

Y_{2}
V_{3}
U_{3}
Z
\propto

and so, as we are assuming that
V_{3}
is full-rank in the sense of
Eq.

8.3
we know that

(8.19)

Contracting both tensor networks against their duals leaving the leftmost leg of
W_{2}
and
\tilde{W}_{2}
open, we conclude that

\propto
C
A_{2}
A_{2}^{\dagger}
C^{\dagger}
W_{2}
W_{2}^{\dagger}
\tilde{W}_{2}^{\dagger}
\tilde{W}_{2}

and so we can use the full-rank assumption shown in
Eq.

8.7
, and
Lemma

8.4
, to conclude that there exist two unitary matrices
C_{1},C_{2}\in\textup{U}(D)
for which
C=C_{1}\otimes C_{2}
, which allows us to rewrite
Eq.

8.19
as

∎

8.2
Quotient tensor network manifold structure

Let us now write the gauge freedom identified in the previous sub-section as a group action. Recall that the tensor network manifold associated with the tensor network family of isometric PEPS on an
L\times(L+1)
lattice with bond dimension
D
and physical dimension
d
is given by

\displaystyle M_{\textup{iso}}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{S}^{2D^{4}-1}\times\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{D^{3}})^{\times 2L-3}\times\textup{V}_{D^{2}}(\mathbb{C}^{dD^{2}})^{\times(L-2)^{2}}

\displaystyle\quad\times\textup{V}_{D^{2}}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}D})^{L-2}\times\textup{V}_{D}(\mathbb{C}^{dD})\times\textup{U}(D^{2})^{\times L-1}.

To ease the notation, let us assume that
d=D
, which allows us to write
M_{\textup{iso}}
as

\displaystyle M_{\textup{iso}}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{S}^{2d^{4}-1}\times\textup{V}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})^{\times 2L-3}\times\textup{V}_{d^{2}}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})^{\times(L-2)(L-1)}\times\textup{V}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}})\times\textup{U}(d^{2})^{\times L-1}.

To describe a tensor network of this family up to a phase, we use

N_{\textup{iso}}:=\mathbb{CP}^{d^{4}-1}\times\textup{PV}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})^{\times 2L-3}\times\textup{PV}_{d^{2}}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})^{\times(L-2)(L-1)}\times\textup{PV}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}})\times\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times L-1},

which we endow with its
natural metric

g_{\textup{iso}}:=g_{\textup{FS}}\oplus g_{pst}^{\oplus L(L-1)}\oplus g_{pu}^{\oplus L-1}
.

Definition 8.6

(Gauge action on isometric PEPS)
.

We define the action of
\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(L^{2}-L)}
on
N_{\textup{iso}}
as

\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(L^{2}-L)}\times N_{\textup{iso}}\to N_{\textup{iso}},\quad(X,(U,V,W))\mapsto(XU,XV,XW),

where
U
and
W
denote the bottom and top rows of the PEPS, respectively, and
V
denotes the bulk of the PEPS.
This way,

\displaystyle U

\displaystyle:=([\Lambda],[U_{1}],\dotsc,[U_{L-1}])\in\mathbb{CP}^{d^{4}-1}\times\textup{PV}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})^{\times L-1},

\displaystyle V

\displaystyle:=(V^{1},\dotsc,V^{L-2}),

\displaystyle W

\displaystyle:=([W_{1}],\dotsc,[W_{L}])\in\textup{PV}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}})\times\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times L-1},

where each
V^{i}
denotes a row of the bulk of the PEPS state, and so

V^{i}:=([V^{i}_{1}],\dotsc,[V^{i}_{L}])\in\textup{PV}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})\times\textup{PV}_{d^{2}}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})^{\times L-1},

for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,L-2\}
. We define
X
as

X:=(X^{1},\dotsc,X^{L}),

where each
X^{i}
acts on a row of the PEPS. Thus,
X^{i}\in\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2L-1}
for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,L-1\}
, and
X^{L}\in\textup{PU}(d)^{\times L-1}
. More explicitly,
X^{1}
acts on
U
,
X^{i}
acts on
V^{i-1}
for every
i\in\{2,\dotsc,L-1\}
and
X^{L}
acts on
W
. The action on the first row (see
Fig.

12
) can be written as

\displaystyle XU

\displaystyle:=X^{1}U

\displaystyle:=([(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{1}_{1}\otimes X^{1}_{2})\Lambda],

\displaystyle\quad[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{1}_{3}\otimes X^{1}_{4})U_{1}(X^{1}_{1})^{\dagger}],\dotsc,[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{1}_{2(L-1)-1}\otimes X^{1}_{2(L-1)})U_{L-2}(X^{1}_{2(L-2)-1})^{\dagger}],

\displaystyle\quad[(\mathds{1}\otimes\mathds{1}\otimes X^{1}_{2L-1})U_{L-1}(X^{1}_{2(L-1)-1})^{\dagger}])\in\mathbb{CP}^{d^{4}-1}\times\textup{PV}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})^{\times L-1}.

In the bulk of the PEPS, represented by
V
,
X
acts as

XV:=(XV^{1},\dotsc,XV^{L-2}),

where for every row
i\in\{2,\dotsc,L-1\}
represented by
V^{i-1}
we define (see
Fig.

13
)

\displaystyle XV^{i-1}

\displaystyle:=([(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{i}_{1}\otimes X^{i}_{2})V^{i-1}_{1}(X^{i-1}_{2})^{\dagger}],

\displaystyle\quad[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{i}_{3}\otimes X^{i}_{4})V^{i-1}_{2}(X^{i}_{1}\otimes X^{i-1}_{4})^{\dagger}],\dotsc,

\displaystyle\quad[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{i}_{2(L-1)-1}\otimes X^{i}_{2(L-1)})V^{i-1}_{L-1}(X^{i}_{2(L-2)-1}\otimes X^{i-1}_{2(L-1)})^{\dagger}],

\displaystyle\quad[(\mathds{1}\otimes\mathds{1}\otimes X^{i}_{2L-1})V^{i-1}_{L}(X^{i}_{2(L-1)-1}\otimes X^{i-1}_{2L-1})^{\dagger}])\in\textup{PV}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})\times\textup{PV}_{d^{2}}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{3}})^{\times L-1}.

Lastly,
X
acts on the last row of the PEPS (see
Fig.

14
) as

\displaystyle XW

\displaystyle:=([(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{L}_{1})W_{1}(X^{L-1}_{2})^{\dagger}],

\displaystyle\quad[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{L}_{2})W_{2}(X^{L}_{1}\otimes X^{L-1}_{4})^{\dagger}],\dotsc,[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{L}_{L-1})W_{L-1}(X^{L}_{L-2}\otimes X^{L-1}_{2(L-1)})^{\dagger}],

\displaystyle\quad[W_{L}(X^{L}_{L-1}\otimes X^{L-1}_{2L-1})^{\dagger}])\in\textup{PV}_{d}(\mathbb{C}^{d^{2}})\times\textup{PU}(d^{2})^{\times L-1}.

This action allows us to obtain the quotient tensor network manifold for which every point is in one-to-one correspondence with a state represented by an isometric PEPS up to a phase. See
Fig.

15
for a visual representation of the setting considered.

Proposition 8.7
.

Let
N_{\textup{iso}}
be endowed with its natural metric
\tilde{g}_{\textup{iso}}
. Consider the action of
\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(L^{2}-L)}
on
N_{\textup{iso}}
as given in
Definition

8.6
. There is a smooth manifold structure and a Riemannian metric
h_{\textup{iso}}
on
B_{\textup{iso}}:=N_{\textup{iso}}/\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(L^{2}-L)}
for which the projection
(N_{\textup{iso}},\tilde{g}_{\textup{iso}})\to(B_{\textup{iso}},h_{\textup{iso}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

Proof.

The action is smooth and isometric as
N_{\textup{iso}}
is endowed with its natural metric. It only remains to see that it is free. To do so, assume that there exists some
X\in\textup{PU}(d)^{\times 2(L^{2}-L)}
and some
(U,V,W)\in N_{\textup{iso}}
for which

(U,V,W)=(XU,XV,XW).

Then, in particular,

W=XW,

and so

\displaystyle[W_{1}]

\displaystyle=[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{L}_{1})W_{1}(X^{L-1}_{2})^{\dagger}],

\displaystyle[W_{i}]

\displaystyle=[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{L}_{i})W_{i}(X^{L}_{i-1}\otimes X^{L-1}_{2i})^{\dagger}],\quad\forall i\in\{2,\dotsc,L-1\}

\displaystyle[W_{L}]

\displaystyle=[W_{L}(X^{L}_{L-1}\otimes X^{L-1}_{2L-1})^{\dagger}]).

From the last equality, it holds that

[X^{L}_{L-1}\otimes X^{L-1}_{2L-1}]=[\mathds{1}],

which implies that

[X^{L}_{L-1}]=[\mathds{1}],\quad\textup{and}\quad[X^{L-1}_{2L-1}]=[\mathds{1}].

Consequently,

[W_{L-1}]=[W_{L-1}(X^{L}_{L-2}\otimes X^{L-1}_{2(L-1)})^{\dagger}],

which means that

[X^{L}_{L-1}]=[\mathds{1}],\quad\textup{and}\quad[X^{L-1}_{2(L-1)}]=[\mathds{1}].

Continuing this reasoning, we conclude that
[X^{L-1}_{2L-1}]=[\mathds{1}]
and

[X^{L}_{i}]=[\mathds{1}],\quad\textup{and}\quad[X^{L-1}_{2i}]=[\mathds{1}]

for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,L-1\}
. Looking now at
X^{L-1}V^{L-2}
we know that

\displaystyle[V^{L-2}_{1}]

\displaystyle=[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{L-1}_{1}\otimes\mathds{1})V^{L-2}_{1}(X^{L-2}_{2})^{\dagger}],

\displaystyle[V^{L-2}_{i}]

\displaystyle=[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{L-1}_{2i-1}\otimes\mathds{1})V^{L-2}_{i}(X^{L-1}_{2i-1}\otimes X^{L-2}_{2i})^{\dagger}],\quad\forall i\in\{2,\dotsc,L-1\},

\displaystyle[V^{L-2}_{L}]

\displaystyle=[V^{L-2}_{L}(X^{L-1}_{2(L-1)-1}\otimes X^{L-2}_{2L-1})^{\dagger}]

from which we deduce that

[X^{L-2}_{2i}]=[\mathds{1}],\quad\textup{and}\quad[X^{L-1}_{2i-1}]=[\mathds{1}],

for every
i\in\{1,\dotsc,L-1\}
. Repeating the same reasoning by
moving downwards
along each row, we find that
X^{i}
consists of the unit element for every
i\in\{2,\dotsc,L\}
, and it only remains to study
X^{1}
. In this case, we know that

\displaystyle[\Lambda]

\displaystyle=[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{1}_{1}\otimes\mathds{1})\Lambda],

\displaystyle[U_{i}]

\displaystyle=[(\mathds{1}\otimes X^{1}_{2(i+1)-1}\otimes\mathds{1})U_{i}(X^{1}_{2i-1})^{\dagger}],

\displaystyle[U_{L-1}]

\displaystyle=[U_{L-1}(X^{1}_{2(L-1)-1})^{\dagger}].

Thus, the same argument as before shows that the action is free. The result then follows from
Proposition

A.9
.
∎

Appendix A
Background in Riemannian geometry

In this section, we will introduce some auxiliary results and definitions that are used in the main text. First, we will give a brief introduction to Riemannian submersions and Lie groups. We will later present the manifolds used to construct the tensor network manifolds studied in this work. Lastly, we will give some results that guarantee that the actions considered in the main text are isometric. We assume previous knowledge on Riemannian manifolds. We refer to
[
16
]
for an introduction to this topic.

A.1
Riemannian submersions

Let us begin with a brief introduction to Riemannian submersions. For an in-depth discussion on this topic, we refer to classic references such as
[
16
]
or O’Neill’s articles
[
21
,
20
]
. Let us first define a
submersion
between Riemannian manifolds.

Definition A.1

(Submersion)
.

Let
M
and
B
be two smooth manifolds, and let
F:M\rightarrow B
be a smooth map. We say that
F
is a
submersion
if its differential
dF|_{p}
is surjective for all
p\in M
.
M
and
B
are often referred to as the
total
and
base
spaces, respectively.

Given a submersion, the tangent space of the total space at each point can be split into its
vertical
and
horizontal
components.

Definition A.2

(Vertical and horizontal tangent spaces)
.

Given a submersion
\pi:M\rightarrow B
, we define the
vertical tangent space
at
p\in M
as
V_{p}M:=\ker d\pi|_{p}
. Note that
V_{p}M
is a vector space of dimension
(n-m)
, where
n
is the dimension of
M
and
m
is the dimension of
B
. This way, if
M
is a Riemannian manifold, we can define the
horizontal tangent space
as
H_{p}M:=(V_{p}M)^{\bot}
. In particular,

T_{p}M=V_{p}M\oplus H_{p}M,

for every
p\in M
.

Riemannian submersions
are submersions which
preserve
the metric between the total and the base space.

Definition A.3

(Riemannian Submersion)
.

Let
(M,g)
and
(B,h)
be two Riemannian manifolds, and let
\pi:M\rightarrow B
be a submersion. We say that
\pi
is a
Riemannian submersion
if for every
p\in M
,
d\pi|_{p}
maps
H_{p}M
isometrically onto
T_{\pi(p)}B
. That is, for each
p\in M
and
X,Y\in H_{p}M
,

\langle X,Y\rangle_{g}=\langle d\pi|_{p}X,d\pi|_{p}Y\rangle_{h}.

One of the most widely studied methods for constructing Riemannian submersions is by considering quotient maps with respect to a group action defined on a Riemannian manifold. This is the setting considered in the main text. Let us begin by defining group actions on manifolds.

Definition A.4

(Group action on a manifold)
.

Let
G
be a group and
M
be a manifold. A
left action
of
G
on
M
is a map
G\times M\to M
, usually denoted as
(x,p)\mapsto x\cdot p
verifying the following:

•

x_{2}\cdot(x_{1}\cdot p)=(x_{2}x_{1})\cdot p
for every
x_{1},x_{2}\in G
,
p\in M
.

•

e\cdot p=p
for every
p\in M
,
e
being the unit of
G
.

Right actions are defined analogously.

Although group actions often give rise to Riemannian submersions, not every group action does. Some sufficient conditions for a group action to give rise to a Riemannian submersion are for the action to be
smooth, free, proper
and
isometric
.

Definition A.5

(Smooth action)
.

The action of a Lie group
G
on a manifold
M
is
smooth
if the map
G\times M\rightarrow M
given by
(x,p)\mapsto x\cdot p
is smooth.

Definition A.6

(Free action)
.

A group action of
G
on a manifold
M
is
free
if for every
p\in M
,

\{x\in G:xp=p\}=\{e\},

where
e
denotes the unit of
G
.

Definition A.7

(Proper action)
.

A group action of
G
on a manifold
M
is said to be
proper
if the map

\displaystyle G\times M

\displaystyle\rightarrow M\times M

\displaystyle(x,p)

\displaystyle\mapsto(x\cdot p,p)

is proper, i.e., the preimage of every compact set is compact.

In particular, every smooth action of a compact Lie group is always proper (cf.
[
16
, Corollary C.16]
).

Definition A.8

(Isometric action)
.

A group action of
G
on a Riemannian manifold
(M,g)
is said to be
isometric
if, for every
x\in G
, the map

\displaystyle\alpha_{x}:M

\displaystyle\to M

\displaystyle p

\displaystyle\mapsto x\cdot p

is an isometry on
(M,g)
(i.e. a diffeomorphism such that for every point
p\in M
and every
u,v\in T_{p}M
,
g(u,v)=g(d\alpha_{p}(u),d\alpha_{p}(v))
(cf.
Definition

A.14
)).

As we mentioned earlier, every group action satisfying the above properties induces a Riemannian submersion.

Proposition A.9

(
[
16
, Corollary 2.29]
)
.

Let
(M,g)
be a Riemannian manifold, and let
G
be a Lie group acting smoothly, freely, properly and isometrically on
M
. Then, the orbit space
M/G
has a unique smooth manifold structure and Riemannian metric such that
\pi:M\rightarrow M/G
is a Riemannian submersion.

A.2
Lie groups

We now introduce some of the most elementary definitions and properties of Lie groups. Although Lie groups can be both studied from the point of view of algebra and differential geometry, we will focus on the latter approach. For a more general and detailed introduction to Lie groups, see for example
[
11
]
.

Definition A.10

(Lie group)
.

A
Lie group
is a group
G
such that it can be endowed with a smooth (real) manifold structure in such a way that both the group operation and the inverse map are smooth.

We consider two Lie groups in this text. The first is the unitary group

\textup{U}(n):=\{U\in\textup{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}):U^{\dagger}U=\mathds{1}\},

endowed with its
bi-invariant
metric, which is given by

g_{\textup{bi}}(X,Y):=\Tr(Y^\dagger X),

for every
U\in\textup{U}(n)
and any
X,Y\in T_{U}\textup{U}(n)
.

The second Lie group considered is the projective unitary group
\textup{PU}(n)
,

\textup{PU}(n):=\{[U]:U\in\textup{U}(n)\},

where
[U]:=\{\lambda U:\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\}
for every
U\in\textup{U}(n)
. While it is well-known that
\textup{U}(n)
is a compact Lie group, to the best of our knowledge the group
\textup{PU}(n)
is not as studied in the literature.
\textup{PU}(n)
is indeed a group with respect to the product defined as

[U]\cdot[V]:=[UV],

for every
[U],[V]\in\textup{PU}(n)
. In order to ensure that it is a
Lie group
, let us first define the concept of
normal subgroup
of a group.

Definition A.11

(Normal subgroup)
.

Let
G
be a group and
H
be a subgroup of
G
. We say that
H
is a
normal subgroup
of
G
if

xH=Hx

for every
x\in G
.

The quotient of a Lie group by one of its closed normal subgroups results in a Lie group.

Theorem A.12

(
[
15
, Theorem 21.26]
)
.

Suppose
G
is a Lie group and
K\subseteq G
is a closed normal subgroup of
G
. Then
G/K
is a Lie group.

From the above result, it is straightforward to conclude that
\textup{PU}(n)
is a Lie group, as it arises as the quotient of
\textup{U}(n)
by its—normal and closed—subgroup

\{\lambda\mathds{1}:\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\},

where
\mathds{1}
denotes the identity matrix of size
n
.

Lastly, observe that the tensor product operation presented in the introduction can be extended to the projected unitary group.

Remark A.13
.

The tensor product map

\displaystyle\textup{U}(n)\times\textup{U}(n)

\displaystyle\to\textup{U}(n^{2})

\displaystyle(X,Y)

\displaystyle\mapsto X\otimes Y,

which corresponds to the restriction of a bi-linear function to the set
\textup{U}(n)\times\textup{U}(n)
, induces a well-defined map on
\textup{PU}(n)\times\textup{PU}(n)
,

\displaystyle\textup{PU}(n)\times\textup{PU}(n)

\displaystyle\to\textup{PU}(n^{2})

\displaystyle([X],[Y])

\displaystyle\mapsto[X\otimes Y].

A.3
Manifolds of interest

Let us now give a short description of the different manifolds that are considered in this work. Every tensor of the tensor network families considered in this work can be seen as a point in the sphere, a unitary matrix or a linear isometry. Thus, the tensor network manifolds studied are obtained by considering the Cartesian product of these three manifolds.

We already saw above that the unitary group is a Lie group, and that the Riemannian metric that we consider for it is the bi-invariant metric. We also consider the sphere
\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
which we understand as a real manifold embedded in
\mathbb{C}^{n}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{2n}
. The metric considered for the sphere is known as the round metric,
g_{\textup{round}}
, which is the one induced by the Euclidean metric on
\mathbb{R}^{2n}

Linear isometries can be seen as complex matrices
U
of size
n\times k
, with
1\leq k\leq n
, such that
U^{\dagger}U=\mathds{1}
. The set of linear isometries from
\mathbb{C}^{k}
to
\mathbb{C}^{n}
,

\textup{V}_{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n}):=\{X\in\textup{M}_{n\times k}:X^{\dagger}X=\mathds{1}\},

can be endowed with a smooth manifold structure (cf.
[
1
]
). The manifold of linear isometries is known as the Stiefel manifold and it can also be understood as the quotient of
\textup{U}(n)
by the group action of
\textup{U}(n-k)
defined as

\textup{U}(n-k)\times\textup{U}(n)\to\textup{U}(n),\quad(X,U)\mapsto U\begin{pmatrix}\mathds{1}&0\\
0&X\end{pmatrix},

(A.1)

where
\mathds{1}
is the identity of size
k
(cf.
[
1
]
). We consider the Stiefel manifold endowed with the metric
g_{\textup{st}}
for which the projection
(\textup{U}(n),g_{\textup{bi}})\to(\textup{V}_{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n}),g_{\textup{st}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

As we mentioned earlier, the tensor network manifolds associated with the tensor network families studied in
Sections

2
to
8
are defined as the product of the above manifolds. The tensor network manifolds are always assumed to be endowed with the product metric, and each component is assumed to be endowed with its corresponding metric (
g_{\textup{bi}}
for the unitary group,
g_{\textup{round}}
round for the sphere and
g_{\textup{st}}
for the Stiefel manifold). We call this product metric the
natural metric
of the tensor network manifold.

In the main text we also considered quotient tensor network manifolds which allowed to describe a tensor network up to a phase. In order to do so, we considered the quotient of the original tensor network manifold by the group action given by the multiplication by a complex phase on each factor of the product.

The manifold that arises when considering the quotient of
\textup{U}(n)
by the multiplication by a complex phase was already studied in
Section

A.2
, and corresponds to the
projective unitary group

\textup{PU}(n)(\simeq\textup{U}(n)/\textup{U}(1))
,

\textup{PU}(n)=\{[U]:U\in\textup{U}(n)\},

where
[U]=\{\lambda U:\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\}
. We consider
\textup{PU}(n)
endowed with the metric
g_{\textup{pu}}
for which the projection
(\textup{U}(n),g_{\textup{bi}})\to(\textup{PU}(n),g_{\textup{pu}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

If we consider the quotient of the sphere
\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
by the multiplication by a complex phase we obtain the
complex projective space

\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}(\simeq\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}/\textup{U}(1))
,

\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}:=\{[z]:z\in\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}\},

where
[z]:=\{\lambda z:\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\}
. We endow
\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}
with the metric
g_{\textup{FS}}
for which the projection
(\mathbb{S}^{2k+1},g_{\textup{round}})\to(\mathbb{CP}^{k},g_{\textup{FS}})
is a Riemannian submersion. This metric is known as the Fubini-Study metric
[
16
]
.

Lastly, when we consider the quotient of the Stiefel manifold by the multiplication by a complex phase we obtain the
projective Stiefel manifold

\textup{PV}_{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n})(\simeq\textup{V}_{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n})/\textup{U}(1))

[
12
]
,

\textup{PV}_{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n}):=\{[X]:X\in\textup{M}_{n\times k}(\mathbb{C}),\ X^{\dagger}X=\mathds{1}\},

where
[X]=\{\lambda X:\lambda\in\textup{U}(1)\}
. Using the definition of the Stiefel manifold from
Eq.

A.1
, we can also rewrite the above description of
\textup{PV}_{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n})
as

\textup{PV}_{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n})=\{[U]:U\in\textup{U}(n)\},

where

[U]=\{\lambda U\begin{pmatrix}\mathds{1}&0\\
0&V\end{pmatrix}:\lambda\in\textup{U}(1),V\in\textup{U}(n-k)\}.

We consider the projective complex Stiefel manifold endowed with the metric
g_{\textup{pst}}
for which the projection
(\textup{U}(n),g_{\textup{bi}})\to(\textup{PV}_{k}(\mathbb{C}^{n}),g_{\textup{pst}})
is a Riemannian submersion.

Again, the quotient tensor network manifolds that arise as the Cartesian product of the projective unitary group, the complex projective space and the projective Stiefel manifold are always endowed with the product of the metrics considered above, also denoted as the
natural metric
.

A.4
Isometric actions

Lastly, let us prove some auxiliary results that will allow us to guarantee that the actions considered in the main text are isometric. We begin by defining an isometry between Riemannian manifolds.

Definition A.14

(Isometry)
.

Let
(M,g)
and
(N,h)
be two Riemannian manifolds. We say that
f:M\to N
is an isometry if
f
is a diffeomorphism and
df_{p}
is an isometry between
T_{p}M
and
T_{f(p)}N
for every
p\in M
, i.e.

g(u,v)=h(df(u),df(v)),

for every
p\in M
and every
u,v\in T_{p}M
.

Next, let us show that left and right multiplication in the unitary group endowed with its bi-invariant metric are isometric actions.

Proposition A.15

(Matrix multiplication is an isometric action on
\textup{U}(n)
)
.

Let
(\textup{U}(n),g_{\textup{bi}})
be the unitary group endowed with its bi-invariant metric. Let
\textup{U}(n)
act on itself by left (resp. right) multiplication. Then, for every
U\in\textup{U}(n)
the map

L_{U}:(\textup{U}(n),g_{\textup{bi}})\to(\textup{U}(n),g_{\textup{bi}}),\quad p\mapsto Up,

(resp.
p\mapsto pU
) is an isometry.

Proof.

Let us prove the result for the left multiplication. The proof for the right multiplication is an analogous.

For every
p\in\textup{U}(n)
and every
v\in T_{p}\textup{U}(n)
, let
\gamma_{p,v}(t)
be the unique geodesic in
\textup{U}(n)
such that
\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p
and
\gamma_{p,v}^{\prime}(0)=v
. Then, we know that

dL_{U}|_{p}(v)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}L_{U}(\gamma_{p,v}(t))=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}U\gamma_{p,v}(t)=U\gamma^{\prime}_{p,v}(0)=Uv,

and so
dL_{U}|_{p}:T_{p}\textup{U}(n)\to T_{Up}\textup{U}(n)
acts by left-multiplication for every
U\in G
and every
p\in\textup{U}(n)
. Therefore, since
U
is unitary,

g_{\textup{bi}}(dL_{U}(v),dL_{U}(w))=g_{\textup{bi}}(Uv,Uw)=\Tr(w^\dagger U^\dagger Uv)=\Tr(w^\dagger v)=g_{\textup{bi}}(v,w),

for every
p\in\textup{U}(n)
and every
v,w\in T_{p}\textup{U}(n)
, concluding the proof.
∎

We will now prove that left multiplication on the sphere by a unitary matrix is also an isometric action, whenever the sphere is endowed with the round metric. To do so, let us first study the round metric on the sphere
\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
, when understood as a subset of
\mathbb{C}^{n}
.

Lemma A.16

(Round metric on the sphere)
.

Let
(\mathbb{S}^{2n-1},g_{\textup{round}})
be the sphere endowed with the round metric. On the one hand, we can see the round sphere embedded in
\mathbb{R}^{2n}
, i.e. every
x\in\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
can be written as

x=(x_{1},y_{1},\dotsc,x_{n},y_{n})^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},

such that
x^{T}x=1
. On the other hand, we can see it as embedded in the complex space
\mathbb{C}^{n}
, i.e. we can write every
\tilde{x}\in\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
as

\tilde{x}=(\tilde{x}_{1}+i\tilde{y}_{1},\dotsc,\tilde{x}_{n}+i\tilde{y}_{n})^{T}\in\mathbb{C}^{n},

such that
\tilde{x}^{\dagger}\tilde{x}=1
. When considering this second picture,
g_{\textup{round}}
can be written as

g_{\textup{round}}(v,w)=\textup{Re}(w^{\dagger}v),

for every
p\in\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
and every
v,w\in T_{p}\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
.

Proof.

When seeing the sphere as embedded in
\mathbb{R}^{2n-1}
, every tangent vector
v
at a point
x
,
v\in T_{x}\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
, can be understood as an element in
\mathbb{R}^{2n}
verifying
v^{T}x=0
. Recall that the round metric is that induced by the Euclidean metric via the inclusion map from the sphere to
\mathbb{R}^{2n}
. For this reason, for every
x\in\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
, the inner product between every two tangent vectors
v,w\in T_{x}\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
is given by

g_{\textup{round}}(v,w)=w^{T}v.

In particular, if we write
v
and
w
in coordinates as

\displaystyle v

\displaystyle=(a_{1},b_{1},\dotsc,a_{n},b_{n})^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},

\displaystyle w

\displaystyle=(c_{1},d_{1},\dotsc,c_{n},d_{n})^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},

we can rewrite their inner product as

g_{\textup{round}}(u,v)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}c_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}d_{i}.

Rewriting this expression using the complex space embedding picture, both
v
and
w
can be written as

\displaystyle\tilde{v}

\displaystyle=(a_{1}+ib_{1},\dotsc,a_{n}+ib_{n})^{T}\in\mathbb{C}^{n},

\displaystyle\tilde{w}

\displaystyle=(c_{1}+id_{1},\dotsc,c_{n}+id_{n})^{T}\in\mathbb{C}^{n},

and their inner product can be written as

g_{\textup{round}}(\tilde{v},\tilde{w})=\textup{Re}(\tilde{w}^{\dagger}\tilde{v})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}c_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}d_{i},

which coincides with that shown above.
∎

Proposition A.17

(Left multiplication by a unitary matrix is an isometric action on the sphere)
.

Let
(\mathbb{S}^{2n-1},g_{\textup{round}})
be the sphere endowed with the round metric. Let
\textup{U}(n)
act on
(\mathbb{S}^{2n-1},g_{\textup{round}})
by left multiplication, seeing the sphere as embedded in
\mathbb{C}^{n}
. Then, for every
U\in\textup{U}(n)
the map

L_{U}:(\mathbb{S}^{2n-1},g_{\textup{round}})\to(\mathbb{S}^{2n-1},g_{\textup{round}}),\quad p\mapsto Up,

is an isometry.

Proof.

Following the same reasoning as in the proof of
Proposition

A.15
we conclude that for every
p\in\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
,
dL_{U}|_{p}:T_{p}\,\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}\to T_{Up}\,\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
also acts by left multiplication, i.e.
dL_{U}|_{p}(v)=Uv
for every
p\in\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
and any
v\in T_{p}\mathbb{S}^{2n-1}
. Moreover,

g_{\textup{round}}(Uv,Uw)=\textup{Re}(w^{\dagger}U^{\dagger}Uv)=\textup{Re}(w^{\dagger}v)=g_{\textup{round}}(v,w),

finishing the proof.
∎

To finish, we show a result that relates isometries and Riemannian submersions.

Proposition A.18
.

Let
\pi:(M,g)\to(B,\tilde{g})
be a Riemannian submersion. Consider an isometry
f:M\to M
for which there exists some function
\tilde{f}:B\to B
fulfilling
\pi\circ f=\tilde{f}\circ\pi
. Then
\tilde{f}
is also an isometry.

Proof.

Let
x\in M
and consider two horizontal vectors
u,v\in H_{x}M
. Since
\pi
is a Riemannian submersion and
f
is an isometry on
(M,g)
we know that

\tilde{g}(d\pi(u),d\pi(v))=g(u,v)=g(df(u),df(v)).

Next, since
\pi\circ f=\tilde{f}\circ\pi
, it follows that
df
preserves the horizontality of vectors. Indeed, for any vertical vector
w\in V_{x}M
, it follows that

d\pi(df(w))=d\tilde{f}(d\pi(w))=d\tilde{f}(0)=0.

Thus, using again that
\pi
is a Riemannian submersion, we know that

g(df(u),df(v))=\tilde{g}(d\pi(df(u)),d\pi(df(v))).

Lastly, since by assumption
\pi\circ f=\tilde{f}\circ\pi
, we conclude that

\tilde{g}(d\pi(df(u)),d\pi(df(v)))=\tilde{g}(d\tilde{f}(d\pi(u)),d\tilde{f}(d\pi(v))),

finishing the proof.
∎

The above result, along with
Propositions

A.15
and
A.17
allow us to conclude that all of the group actions considered in the main text are isometric.
